title: A different starting point for conflict
objective: Settle a disagreement by checking facts before positions; decide what can go ahead and what must be verified first
learn: How to separate evidence from explanation, check disputed wording with its owner, and weigh accuracy against the time residents have to respond

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: In a disagreement, the first decision often happens before anyone speaks. If I decide that a colleague is trying to make me look careless, I will collect evidence for my defense. If I decide I need to understand what they saw, I will ask a different first question. Both responses may follow the same email. The interpretation I carry into the conversation changes what information I can gather and what we can accomplish.

teaching.title: Find the interest behind the position
teaching.text:
Suppose an intake specialist wants another review before letters go out. A supervisor wants the letters mailed the same day. Each can make a defensible case, and neither proposal explains what is at stake. Ask the specialist to describe the last problem a review would have caught. Ask the supervisor what happens to a person waiting another day. One may be protecting people from an incorrect instruction and the other may be protecting their time to act. Both interests can now guide a decision.

Use neutral language for the shared problem. “How can we catch conflicting instructions and still give people time to respond?” offers both people real work to do. They could check only letters with conflicting dates, change the template at its source, or test a review at an earlier point. Before choosing, identify what evidence would make each option reasonable. A disagreement about the facts might require looking at a sample before anyone can responsibly recommend a fix.

teaching.title: Notice when the conversation changes
teaching.text:
Catch the moment you start rehearsing a rebuttal or assigning motives. Ask yourself which part of your account the other person could verify and which part only they could explain. You can stay firm about an observed consequence while leaving the explanation open. Understanding the reason for a proposal also makes it easier to say why you cannot accept it.

After the decision, return to both interests. Did people get accurate instructions? Did they receive them in time? If the answer differs between the two, invite the colleague back to interpret what happened. Joint problem solving lasts beyond a cordial meeting when both people can influence what gets tried next.

teaching.title: What each side is protecting
teaching.text:
Return to the decision about releasing the letters. The person responsible for the deadline has a good reason to ask what another review would accomplish. The person requesting a review has a good reason to ask what happens to a resident who acts on the wrong date. Each can make a mistake about the other. “They are delaying the mailing” and “They don't care whether the letters are accurate” both leave out the competing duty. Ask each person what they believe would happen if the team adopted the other person's proposal today. Those answers reveal which risks they are actually comparing.

A facilitator using a participative approach can invite the group to examine one disputed letter together. Mark the sentence the reviewer considers ambiguous and ask the deadline owner to read it as a resident would. If both readings are plausible, agree on what would resolve the question and who can decide. If the disagreement concerns an authoritative due date, send the question to the person who can establish it. A collaborative process can uncover the problem. It cannot confer authority to settle a question that belongs elsewhere.

teaching.title: Choose your next response by what is at stake
teaching.text:
The exercise changes if a junior reviewer tells you that the lead routinely mocks people who flag errors. The accuracy question still needs an answer. The employee has also raised a concern about conduct and the cost of speaking. Asking the two people to work out the mailing decision together could expose the reviewer to more of the behavior they described. A supervisor can arrange coverage for the mailing, speak privately with the employee and seek guidance through the appropriate workplace process. A colleague without supervisory authority can help the person identify a route for the concern without volunteering them for a public discussion.

Use Leading through conflict across difference in People, Access and Culture to prepare two openings for this case. In one, the team has competing work priorities. In the other, a staff member has raised a possible conduct concern. Name the evidence that changed your decision. A peer can then play the person with less authority and tell you which of your words allowed them to correct your interpretation. The competency is visible when the leader can revise both the explanation of a conflict and the response it calls for.

scenario: Two letters in a mailing give different dates. The reviewer wants another check. The mailing lead sees residents losing another day to respond.
decision: What do you let go forward while the deadline is verified?

choices.label: Pause only the affected letters and ask the person responsible for the deadline to confirm it.
choices.feedback: Residents with clear letters retain time. Someone must identify which versions contain the disputed wording and tell staff when a decision is due.

choices.label: Hold the mailing briefly and test whether the conflicting date appears in more than one version.
choices.feedback: You could catch errors outside the first sample. Set a deadline for widening or narrowing the hold so a precaution does not quietly become a delay for everyone.

perspective: A worker who answers calls explains that people often receive two versions in one household. Each letter can read clearly on its own while the pair gives conflicting directions.
reconsider: Which comparison would change the scope of the hold? Who can confirm the date before the next print run?
reflection: Which duty did you assume the other colleague cared less about?
transfer: In a second fictional mailing, list the two interests and one piece of evidence that could change each person's position.
followup: Check the disputed wording with its owner and compare accuracy and time left for residents to respond.

title: Career choices at the top of a job class
objective: Help a top-of-range specialist sort out pay, classification and growth; choose which concern to raise first
learn: How to spot a lasting change in duties, ask what the employee wants, and when a classification review or a move fits

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: An experienced specialist can love the daily work and still have a serious question about pay. Reaching the top of a salary range changes what the current position can offer. It does not settle whether the work itself has changed, whether another specialist role would fit, or whether managing people is an attractive use of the next ten years. Each of those questions deserves its own conversation.

teaching.title: Understand what has changed in the work
teaching.text:
Start with two or three recurring responsibilities. Describe the decisions you make, whose work depends on them, and what judgment the job now requires. More cases of the same complexity demonstrate workload. Designing a method that several units rely on may raise a different question about the scope of the position. The distinction matters because classification concerns the work assigned, while a performance conversation also considers how well an individual does it.

For example, a policy specialist might have progressed from answering questions about established guidance to resolving new interpretations across programs. Identify who assigns that responsibility and how frequently it occurs. Bring a few work examples and the current position description to a supervisor or HR professional. Ask how to request a review where appropriate and what the applicable agreement or plan says. A classification review considers the position and its context. Its outcome cannot be promised.

teaching.title: Choose a path that addresses the actual concern
teaching.text:
If compensation is the main concern, ask for current salary ranges and what a temporary higher-level assignment or special project would mean under the applicable terms. Know the duties, duration, selection process and pay before accepting. A mentor, a professional community or a chance to teach others can deepen influence. Those experiences serve a different purpose from paid advancement.

If supervision is an option, talk with someone who does the job about staffing, feedback, competing priorities and how much time remains for technical work. Then compare a real supervisory opening with a real specialist opening. Your decision should reflect the work you want and the compensation available, with enough information to see what each path would cost you.

teaching.title: Distinguish a classification question from a retention decision
teaching.text:
An employee who has handled unusually complex cases for years can have two legitimate concerns. The classification may no longer describe the duties, and the employee may be ready to earn more even if it does. Treat them as two questions. For the first, compare typical assignments over time with the decisions the position is now expected to make. Ask who holds final authority, how broadly its decisions apply and whether unusual assignments have become a recurring part of the job. Obtain advice from Human Resources about how the relevant classification or compensation question can be considered. Avoid promising a particular finding.

For the second, let the employee say which features of a move are negotiable. A higher salary might matter more than a preferred program area. A predictable schedule might matter more than title. A role that centers supervision could trade away the direct technical work the employee wants to keep. A manager can ask what would make staying worthwhile and relay what they learn to the people who control staffing choices. Being candid about the limits of the current role leaves the employee free to make an informed decision.

teaching.title: Give an experienced specialist a meaningful choice
teaching.text:
In Career Pathways, Succession and Advancement, choose the perspective of the employee whose knowledge colleagues rely on. Imagine she is offered responsibility for training two successors. Before accepting, she asks how much existing work the assignment displaces, who will take over routine questions, whether she can shape the work and how the contribution will be recognized. Sharing expertise is valuable, but someone can spend an entire year onboarding others and have no time left to pursue the development they originally requested. Discuss an alternative that gives her something new to learn as well.

A coaching approach is useful when the employee is exploring possibilities. Take a more explicit approach when only management can explain what work will be removed or which roles exist. A supervisor could arrange for the specialist to meet the manager of a different program and observe a decision there. Afterward, ask what appealed to her, what she would miss and whether a lateral move would broaden the work she can compete for later. An exploration is worthwhile even when the employee decides to stay. End the conversation with one agreed action for the employee and one the supervisor can deliver. Record pay or classification questions separately so they receive an actual answer.

scenario: An experienced specialist reaches the top of the salary range. They now resolve interpretation questions that once went to a different unit. Their manager suggests applying to supervise.
decision: How would you begin a career conversation that could lead to a concrete next step?

choices.label: Ask which work changed, who assigned it, and how often it now occurs.
choices.feedback: You can distinguish sustained duties from occasional cover and bring useful examples to the appropriate review. Compensation or career interests may still need a separate conversation.

choices.label: Ask what the specialist wants to gain, then compare the actual duties of a supervisory and a specialist opportunity.
choices.feedback: The employee can test whether people management fits their interests. Also record whether the current duties themselves warrant a discussion with HR.

perspective: The specialist values solving technical questions and likes teaching colleagues. They want recognition for decisions they already own and have no interest in conducting performance reviews.
reconsider: Which conversation would you have first? What outcome can you realistically promise to follow up on?
reflection: Did you treat advancement as synonymous with supervising?
transfer: Sketch two next steps for this specialist. Give each one an owner and a review date.
followup: Identify a recurring change in duties and ask what the employee hopes to gain before exploring a review or a move.

title: Explaining the value of your work
objective: Describe your work so each listener knows when to involve you
learn: How to adjust the same explanation for a director and a resident, and how to make clear who decides an individual case

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: At a cross-program meeting, introductions can turn into lists of titles and acronyms. A colleague who hears your title may still have no idea when to call you. A value statement connects the work you do well with what gives it meaning for you. It can guide a career decision as well as a conversation. An elevator pitch draws on the statement to help someone quickly understand who you are, what you contribute and what you hope to do next.

teaching.title: Start with something another person could recognize
teaching.text:
Choose a recent piece of work you can discuss without identifying anyone receiving services. Write down who needed help, what they were trying to do and the part you played. Be precise about your contribution. A team might have rewritten an entire packet, while you specifically traced the conflicting instructions and checked the revision with people who answer calls. Both details belong to the team’s story. Only the latter describes what you can offer the next project.

A possible value statement is, “I find my work meaningful when I help people make decisions using instructions they can understand. I help program teams spot the places where our letters leave the next step unclear.” Use it when comparing two job openings. Which would let you exercise that strength, in an environment where the work you value gets time and support? Revisit the statement when experience changes your answer.

teaching.title: Give the introduction a destination
teaching.text:
For an audience of supervisors, add an example and a reason to keep talking. “On a recent revision I compared the instructions on a letter with the steps staff actually use. We found two different deadlines. If your team is changing a notice, I can help check it before it goes out.” For a conversation about career development, the same experience can lead to a different ending. “I’d like to learn how the policy team decides which deadline applies.”

Prepare a spoken version of roughly twenty to thirty seconds. Use a few keywords to practice it in your own voice. Ask a colleague what contribution they heard and whether the invitation was clear. When you use it in conversation, leave time for the listener to answer. Respond to what they say. Eye contact, posture and facial expressions vary across people and cultures and give limited evidence about their interest.

teaching.title: Decide what the introduction is asking the listener to do
teaching.text:
An effective introduction changes with the person hearing it. A new coworker needs to know when to involve you. A leader choosing a project team needs to know what part of the work you can take on. A community partner may reasonably want to know whether you can act on the information they give you. Before speaking, finish this sentence for yourself: “After this conversation, I hope this person can decide whether to …” If you have three different endings, choose the one that fits this encounter.

Consider a staff member who translates findings from service reviews into usable instructions. To a program director, she might say, “I trace where people get stuck after they receive a letter. I can bring you two places where changing the next step would save a second call.” At a community session that introduction could sound like an offer to settle a specific case. She might say instead, “I work on how our letters explain what happens next. I can take concerns about the instructions back to the writing team. Our service staff can help with an individual decision.” Each introduction gives the listener a reasonable expectation and an opening to respond.

teaching.title: Make values specific enough to guide a choice
teaching.text:
Leading With Purpose and Values offers a place to examine the promise behind your introduction. Suppose the value you name is accuracy. A mailing is due at noon and an unresolved question affects only a few versions. What does accuracy require of you? One answer would be to flag exactly which versions need a decision, establish who can supply it and offer a way for the unaffected work to continue. A second value, timely service, now has a place in the choice. A declaration becomes credible when colleagues can recognize it in what you do under competing demands.

Ask two people who know different parts of your work to listen to the introduction and tell you what they would call you about. If one thinks you approve policy and the other thinks you only proofread, revise the words that created those expectations. Practice speaking at a pace you can sustain and prepare a written version for settings where an introduction happens through chat or email. Return to it when your duties or priorities change. The aim is a truthful account of what you currently contribute and the work you are ready to try.

scenario: You improve public notices by tracing confusing instructions. At a program meeting you have thirty seconds to introduce yourself. A resident later asks whether you can fix a particular case.
decision: Which introduction would you use with the resident?

choices.label: Explain the kinds of notice problems you investigate and help the resident find the person who owns the case decision.
choices.feedback: The resident learns what you can take back and who can answer the case question. Check that the next contact is usable.

choices.label: Ask what the resident was trying to do when the notice failed, then explain the boundary of your role.
choices.feedback: You learn which problem matters to the resident. Acknowledge any immediate deadline and connect them with the appropriate service contact.

perspective: The resident says they can read the notice. They cannot tell whether replying to you counts as replying to the program.
reconsider: How would you revise a sentence so this person knows what still needs to happen?
reflection: What might a listener reasonably assume when you say you “handle notices”?
transfer: Write separate two-sentence introductions for a director and a resident. Underline what each listener could do next.
followup: Each listener should be able to say when to involve you and who has authority over an individual case.

title: Getting support for professional development
objective: Turn a vague development request into one a supervisor can decide
learn: How to name the skill to practice, who covers urgent work, and when an answer is needed

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: An employee asks for development and hears, “Let’s come back to that.” It is easy for both parties to leave believing the other one owns the next step. The employee may hear a refusal, while the supervisor may have an unresolved coverage question or a different view of the skill to develop first. A specific request lets them discover which issue actually stands in the way.

teaching.title: Prepare a decision your supervisor can make
teaching.text:
Name the skill, the experience you want and the time or funding it would require. Explain where the team could use the skill, and bring one example of work that shows your preparation. Suppose a staff member who answers program questions wants to learn facilitation. A request to observe an upcoming partner meeting, draft the agenda for the following session and receive feedback from the chair gives the supervisor something concrete to consider.

Include the cost to the team. Who would handle urgent questions while you attend? Which work could wait? If the preferred opportunity costs money, identify the deadline for a decision and a lower-cost option that develops the same skill. Sometimes a short assignment alongside a colleague will give you more useful practice than sitting through a course. Sometimes formal instruction is necessary before you attempt a task. Say why you chose the option you did.

teaching.title: Make room for an honest answer
teaching.text:
If the answer is “not yet,” ask what needs to change. Coverage for one afternoon, evidence of readiness and a restriction on spending call for different responses. For a readiness concern, ask to see an example of the expected work and agree on a chance to demonstrate it. Record the next step and date in your development plan so the request can survive a busy month.

Meanwhile, colleagues, mentors, employee groups and professional communities can help you understand the work you want and identify learning options. Find out what participation requires before committing agency time. If you supervise, state the criteria you use across the team and revisit declined requests. Employees should be able to find an opportunity even when they do not already know the person who offers it.

If an immediate release from duties would leave a shift uncovered, explore a community of practice where colleagues solve similar problems or an employee resource group that offers professional connections. Ask a member what participants actually do and what time the commitment takes, then agree with your supervisor which activities fit paid work time and which require advance approval.

teaching.title: Design a development request that fits the decision
teaching.text:
A supervisor may support an employee’s goal yet have no authority to fund the requested course. Another may control the funds but have no practical way to cover a shift. Ask which constraint applies before reworking the proposal. Consider an employee who wants to learn how to facilitate a discussion in which several programs disagree. A paid class, observing a skilled facilitator and leading fifteen minutes of a real meeting each teach something different. Describe which part the employee needs to practice, what support it takes and what the team receives. Offering a cheaper class helps little if it provides no opportunity to do the work.

An employee can bring a recent example of work completed well and identify the next skill the assignment would demand. A supervisor can explain whether there is a performance concern that needs attention, give a specific example and tell the employee how progress will be judged. Separate that conversation from general encouragement to be patient. If there is no concern about performance, say so. Someone who repeatedly hears “later” may otherwise spend months trying to correct a problem no one actually identified.

teaching.title: Notice who has to make the case
teaching.text:
Use Equitable access to stretch assignments and promotion to look at the same request from the person who allocates development time. Two staff members do similar work. One hears about an opportunity in a standing meeting with managers. The other works the evening shift and learns about it after the deadline. A coach can help either prepare a stronger request. The supervisor also controls who hears about opportunities, whether release time is available and what applicants are asked to show. Improving those conditions gives good coaching a chance to matter.

For an upcoming assignment, decide what has to be announced, how people on each shift will hear about it and how the decision will be explained. Offer preparation to people who have never taken a public assignment before. Ask the employee to come back after the selection. If they did not get it, explain which criterion made the difference and whether another supervised practice is available. If they did, identify whose work covers the time. Follow up after the first attempt to see what they learned and what the experience cost their colleagues. That makes development a decision about the work of a whole team.

scenario: An employee wants practice facilitating a meeting. Their request has twice been postponed. The next partner discussion is on a busy intake day.
decision: What would make the request actionable?

choices.label: Ask to lead the fifteen-minute discussion before the partner decides, and propose cover for urgent calls.
choices.feedback: The supervisor can consider the actual decision, timing and cost. Identify who will give feedback on the facilitation.

choices.label: Ask to shadow the decision, then chair the next one with a named observer.
choices.feedback: This creates a two-step learning route. Verify that the later meeting still has a choice open to participants.

perspective: The supervisor says they support the assignment. The budget owner approves release time and the meeting chair sets the agenda. Neither has heard the request.
reconsider: Which decision belongs to each person? What would you change before asking again?
reflection: When has an encouraging answer obscured who can actually say yes?
transfer: Before the next practice opportunity, prepare a request naming the decision, cover, feedback and last useful date for an answer.
followup: Identify the specific meeting decision to practice, who would cover urgent work, and when an answer is needed.

title: Growing as an individual contributor
objective: Find leadership practice while staying in a technical role
learn: How to choose an assignment that builds influence, name who approves a change, and make room in ordinary duties

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A supervisor’s job changes the substance of a workday. More time goes to coaching, work assignments, performance and decisions about the team. If the part you value most is tracing a policy problem until you can explain it clearly, another position with deeper technical work might fit better. You can make that decision deliberately, and you can revisit it when your interests or circumstances change.

teaching.title: Investigate what a move would give you
teaching.text:
Think about the last month. Which tasks gave you energy even when they were difficult? Where did colleagues turn to you, and what did they ask you to do? Maybe the pleasure came from teaching a new colleague, or from solving the problem yourself. Those experiences can look similar from the outside. The distinction helps you decide whether to explore supervision, a specialist role, project leadership or a lateral move into a different part of state service.

Consider someone who understands disability services and enjoys translating technical guidance. A communications assignment could develop editorial judgment. A program implementation project could develop expertise in applying the same guidance across settings. Conduct an informational interview with someone in each role. Ask them to describe yesterday’s work, a difficult decision and how their success is judged. Check actual job descriptions and compensation before assuming that either move brings advancement in pay.

teaching.title: Test a direction within a manageable assignment
teaching.text:
Choose a bounded opportunity, such as co-leading two meetings of a community of practice or producing one staff guide. Agree on time, responsibilities and the feedback you need. Ask the supervisor which existing tasks can shift during the assignment. That makes room to learn and gives you useful evidence about the amount and kind of work involved.

Keep a short account of what you produced, who used it, and which skills transferred from your current role. Share credit with colleagues and discuss the experience during your next development conversation. A successful experiment can point to a new position. It can also show you which responsibilities you want more of in the role you already hold.

teaching.title: Find the decisions a specialist can influence
teaching.text:
A lateral move can offer more room for judgment even when the pay range stays the same. Investigate the decisions someone in the role actually makes. A specialist who revises service guidance may discover problems on the phones, decide which examples staff need and recommend language to a policy owner. They may have little authority over whether the finished guidance is adopted. Ask a person doing the job to describe a recent disagreement, who settled it and what happened next. Those details show what technical leadership feels like on an ordinary day.

If you want to influence a decision while someone else holds approval, use Leading Without Formal Authority. Consider an experienced worker who notices that three teams teach the same process differently. They can collect examples, locate the point where the instructions diverge and ask which team has responsibility for the decision. Bringing a finished policy draft to the first meeting may invite a debate about who authorized the work. Bringing the contradictory instructions gives the owner a reason to act and allows the specialist to offer expertise where it helps.

teaching.title: Choose an opportunity that develops judgment
teaching.text:
A specialist role can become a collection of rescue assignments because an experienced employee is the person everyone trusts to finish difficult work. Ask what a proposed assignment adds to your abilities. If the answer is another chance to perform the same task under greater pressure, it may be an urgent contribution while offering little development. For the guidance project, ask to observe how the owner weighs conflicting interpretations or lead a small trial of revised instructions. Either develops judgment that routine editing alone would leave untouched.

Agree up front about who will present the result, who receives credit for each contribution and what part of the specialist’s existing workload will move. Then keep a short record of the decision you influenced, the information you supplied and what the decision maker did with it. If the recommendation was declined, ask what additional evidence would have made a difference. You may discover a knowledge gap worth addressing or a constraint beyond the role’s control. When an opportunity in another unit appears, your record can help you judge whether it offers different responsibilities you actually want, as well as explain the contribution you can already make.

scenario: Three teams teach the same service instruction differently. An experienced specialist is offered two ways to help. They want more responsibility while continuing technical work.
decision: Which assignment would teach the specialist a new kind of leadership judgment?

choices.label: Compare three instructions and lead a discussion with the owner about which difference affects residents.
choices.feedback: The specialist can influence the decision and learn which evidence the owner trusts. They need protected time and access to the owner.

choices.label: Test one draft with the people who use it and report what is still unclear.
choices.feedback: The specialist can see whether the explanation works across settings. Clarify who will decide when test results conflict.

perspective: The specialist already corrects drafts every week. Their goal is to learn how a recommendation survives disagreement between units.
reconsider: What part of either assignment would give them a decision they have not previously exercised?
reflection: Which parts of the work do you enjoy enough to grow into?
transfer: Choose a one-month stretch assignment and identify what current task would shift to make room.
followup: Name the decision they can influence, who can approve a change, and which ordinary duties would make room for the assignment.

title: Taking the lead in your own career
objective: Test a career interest with a short real assignment
learn: How to pick a question about the work, gather evidence by doing it, and let that evidence shape your next step

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A supervisor may know which assignments need attention this quarter and still know very little about the work you hope to do two years from now. You have information they need. Your interests, strengths and commitments help explain which opportunities are worth pursuing. They have information you need about the work, the capacity to release you and the standards you would need to meet. Career development works better when both sides bring something specific.

teaching.title: Make an interest concrete enough to investigate
teaching.text:
Begin with an occasion when you were absorbed in the work. A staff member says they enjoyed helping a cross-program group explain an eligibility change. Was it interpreting policy, listening to residents’ questions, or coordinating people with different expertise? Each could point to a different path. Write down what you contributed and which part you would choose to do again. Ask two colleagues who saw the work what they think you did well and what took more support.

Choose a question you can answer in a month. For instance, “Do I want more work facilitating discussions where staff disagree about an interpretation?” Arrange to shadow an experienced facilitator, with appropriate permission, and ask what preparation and follow-up the meeting required. The quieter parts of a job often tell you more about fit than the most visible hour does.

teaching.title: Ask for one opportunity and use what you learn
teaching.text:
Bring the question, the evidence you have and a request to your supervisor. You could offer to plan fifteen minutes of a guidance discussion, agree in advance on what the facilitator will observe and debrief afterward. If a different program hosts the opportunity, confirm coverage and timing with the people who can authorize them. Mentors and professional networks can open conversations, while supervisors can make work time and accountability clear.

When you return, describe what changed your mind. Perhaps you liked preparing questions but found the live facilitation less satisfying than anticipated. That is a useful result. Revise the next experience toward the work that interests you and name the support you need to test it further.

teaching.title: Build relationships that can answer different career questions
teaching.text:
Advice, opportunities and sponsorship are different forms of support. A mentor might describe what it takes to lead a public meeting under pressure. A manager with assignment authority can give you a chance to practice and arrange coverage. A sponsor might tell a decision maker that your work deserves consideration and explain why. One person can do more than one of these things, but a good relationship does not automatically give someone the power or willingness to open a particular door. Be specific about what you are asking them to do.

Use Mentoring and sponsorship across difference to examine whose experience informs your view of an opportunity. Suppose two people you admire have both reached leadership through temporary project assignments. Ask how each one heard about the assignment, who covered their ordinary duties and whether the decision makers already knew their work. Their answers may reveal that an informal introduction mattered as much as individual preparation. That is useful knowledge for an employee seeking a fair route into the work and for a manager deciding whether the next opportunity should be announced more broadly.

teaching.title: Decide what evidence would change your direction
teaching.text:
Take a career interest such as working directly with community partners. Arrange a conversation with someone who prepares meetings and someone who follows up when the agency cannot offer what participants requested. The appealing public event may occupy two hours of a week otherwise spent making arrangements, resolving accessibility questions and bringing unwelcome answers back to people. Ask which part they value and where they most often need help. Come away with a more accurate picture of the work and one specific way to test whether it suits you.

A promising experiment could be taking responsibility for reporting back after one session, with a lead checking that the account accurately reflects the discussion. Decide in advance what you hope to learn about yourself. Did you enjoy tracing a concern to someone who could decide it? Were you willing to make another call when there was no satisfying answer? Ask a partner or colleague whether your follow-up left them knowing what would happen next. Use those answers to update the goal. If the experience points you toward analysis or operations instead, you have learned something valuable while making a useful contribution.

scenario: After a community meeting you tell your manager you want more partnership work. You enjoyed both facilitating the conversation and working out how the team would respond afterward.
decision: Which short assignment would help you test that interest?

choices.label: Lead a bounded agenda item and ask someone to watch how you handle disagreement.
choices.feedback: You can compare preparation and facilitation with your initial expectations. Pick a decision participants can still influence.

choices.label: Own the report back to a partner whose suggestion the program could only partly adopt.
choices.feedback: You test whether you enjoy the follow-through and negotiation that partnership requires. Agree who can verify the response before you send it.

perspective: The partner says the public meeting took one hour. Months later, the most valuable contact was the person who explained what changed and what did not.
reconsider: What would you add to your career experiment after hearing that account?
reflection: Which part of a visible role may be difficult to see from outside it?
transfer: Identify a question about a role and one assignment that could change your answer within a month.
followup: Choose a question about the work and evidence from doing it that could change your preference.

title: How colleagues come to trust your leadership
objective: Recognize when a decision broke a promise people relied on; repair trust with those affected
learn: Why dependable processes build trust, how to revisit a missed opportunity openly, and how to make the next selection fair across shifts

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: Two people can trust different things about the same supervisor. One trusts her technical judgment because her interpretation of complex guidance holds up. Another trusts her to take a concern seriously because she has followed up when raising it was uncomfortable. The first is confidence in competence and reliability, often called cognitive trust. The second grows from the experience of care, often called affective trust. Leadership depends on what colleagues repeatedly experience in both respects.

teaching.title: Look at trust at three levels
teaching.text:
Between two people, a missed promise has a particular history. Across a team, staff also watch whose questions receive a response, whose mistakes get discussed in public and who can safely disagree. At the organizational level, people compare what leaders say about fairness with how decisions are actually made. A warm relationship with one supervisor may coexist with serious doubts about an agency process. Ask what exactly people are being asked to trust.

Suppose a supervisor invites staff to apply for a development assignment, then fills it before the stated deadline. One person had planned to apply. Others conclude future announcements might be equally unreliable. The person selected now faces questions about a decision they did not control. Even if the supervisor faced an urgent deadline, saying so privately to a trusted colleague cannot address the wider effect.

teaching.title: Repair the part others can observe
teaching.text:
Acknowledge the discrepancy to the people who received the invitation. Explain what happened, take responsibility for the decision within your control, and identify what can still be corrected. If a remedy requires consultation, say when people will hear the answer. Listen for consequences you missed, including the effect on the selected employee. A response can preserve privacy and still account for the decision.

Then make the next selection dependable. Publish the decision date and criteria, assign someone to track commitments and report back if circumstances change. Ask a colleague outside your usual circle whether the next process worked as described. Your reputation for leadership develops through evidence like this. People deciding whether to rely on you for a bigger responsibility have something more durable than an impression to go on.

teaching.title: Diagnose the promise that failed
teaching.text:
A team can survive an unwelcome decision when it understands how the decision was made. A broken promise about the process has a different cost. In the early selection described here, some employees will question whether future deadlines are dependable. Others may conclude that people who already have access to the decision maker get special treatment. The supervisor cannot know which conclusion an employee reached without asking. More importantly, the supervisor can do something about the broken commitment before asking staff to explain the personal cost of it.

Use Repairing trust after harm to prepare a conversation with someone affected by the decision. Say which commitment you made, what action contradicted it and what you can still change. Ask what consequence you have overlooked. An employee may tell you that the missed assignment was the only occasion this year to demonstrate a skill for another role. A correction to the announcement does little about that lost opportunity. Explore what is within your authority to restore and what you must take to another decision maker. Be equally clear about who will communicate the answer if the original selection has to stand.

teaching.title: Work at the level where confidence needs rebuilding
teaching.text:
In a new project group, colleagues may be willing to rely on each other after several small, accurate handoffs. In a long-standing team, an unacknowledged breach can weaken years of goodwill. Colleagues outside your team may see a question about the organization’s credibility if they have watched similar decisions recur under several supervisors. Each problem calls for different evidence of repair. For a handoff, do what you said by the day promised. For an allocation process, make the next opportunity and its selection criteria visible to everyone eligible. For a recurring pattern, bring the examples to someone able to review decisions across teams.

Ethical leadership means accepting responsibility for keeping a fair commitment even when doing so inconveniences a favored applicant or draws attention to your own mistake. A participative approach can bring staff into designing a better process, provided the supervisor still owns the original decision. Give the group a date when it can see what happened at the next selection. Ask a colleague who had no advance notice of the opening to describe how they learned of it. Their experience gives you a more informative measure of trustworthiness than your own confidence that the new process is fair.

scenario: A supervisor advertised an acting opportunity through Friday and filled it on Thursday. The selected colleague has accepted. An evening employee read the invitation on Friday and wants an explanation.
decision: What repair can the supervisor begin now?

choices.label: Contact affected staff about the early choice, find out what opportunity was lost, and check what can still be corrected.
choices.feedback: Acknowledgment makes the breach visible. Consult the person authorized to determine what remedies are available before promising a new selection.

choices.label: Set up a dependable notice and decision date for the next assignment, then invite the overlooked worker to explain what else remains unresolved.
choices.feedback: A visible process can build confidence over time. It may leave the original harm untouched if the next opportunity is much later.

perspective: The evening worker had already arranged cover and was relying on this assignment for a development goal. The selected colleague says coworkers are questioning their legitimacy.
reconsider: Who needs an answer about the process, and whose personal information must stay private?
reflection: What promise would matter most from the perspective of each employee?
transfer: For the next two opportunities, compare the announced deadline, actual decision time and time each shift received notice.
followup: Revisit the missed opportunity with those affected and make the next deadline and selection process dependable across shifts.

title: Managing your reaction during conflict and change
objective: Stay steady when plans shift suddenly; tell staff what they can act on today
learn: How to separate a decision staff can make now from a question still being checked, and how to promise and keep a time for follow-up

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A supervisor learns that an expected program change has moved forward by a month. Within minutes, staff are asking whether they can honor appointments already on the calendar. The supervisor feels pressure to give a definitive answer. That pressure matters because a quick assurance from someone with authority can become the instruction a whole team follows, even when the supervisor intended it as a guess.

teaching.title: Recognize your own first response
teaching.text:
Some people speed up when surprised. Others go quiet, make a joke or explain the decision before hearing the question. Look back at an occasion when your first reaction made it harder to learn what was happening. What did you do? What might the people present reasonably have concluded? A person who saw the exchange can help you reconstruct it. Give them a narrow question, such as whether you allowed enough time for a second concern.

In the appointment example, a useful first response could be, “I know the start date changed. I don’t have an answer about appointments. Which decisions have to be made today?” Write down urgent questions and give a time for the next update. This keeps responsibility with the leader while staff have a chance to supply information the leader cannot see. If you need a minute to gather your thoughts, say when you will return and follow through.

teaching.title: Use reflection to change the next encounter
teaching.text:
After the immediate demand passes, identify one part of your response you want to practice. A colleague could role-play an employee challenging the next announcement. Try asking what they are trying to protect before explaining what you know. Notice whether you can still hear the answer when it challenges a decision you supported. A change-management framework can help you anticipate which questions will recur as work shifts.

Where you have already given an inaccurate assurance, return to the people who heard it, correct the instruction and ask what decisions they made on its strength. Over time, patterns may point to a need for coaching, peer support or employee assistance. Seeking that help gives you another place to work through your reaction while your team gets the guidance it needs.

teaching.title: Separate your response from the size of the decision
teaching.text:
A leader who becomes very quiet under pressure may look untroubled to one colleague and unavailable to another. A leader who thinks aloud may sound as though a decision has already been made. Learn how your own habits land. Ask a colleague who has seen you handle an unexpected update to describe the first thing you did and what they thought they were supposed to do next. You need observable details to practice with. “You were tense” tells you less than “You said we should cancel the meetings, so I started calling people.”

Some changes call for a clear temporary direction. Others allow people affected to help design the response. In the appointment example, a supervisor can direct staff to hold afternoon appointments open while the new timetable is checked. Once the immediate risk passes, bring scheduling staff and service partners together to decide how to communicate the change. These are distinct leadership choices, even when both occur within an hour. Under pressure it is easy to carry the first choice into the second meeting and announce a plan before the people with operational knowledge have spoken.

teaching.title: Rehearse while the decision is still reversible
teaching.text:
Emotional Intelligence: Understanding Emotions and Choosing a Response gives you a place to practice the interval between noticing a reaction and acting on it. Make a short record of one moment from the example. What did you know at the time? What did you expect would happen if you waited? Whose reaction were you trying to manage? Write a response that gives staff something usable while preserving room to correct an assumption. Say it aloud and have a colleague restate which actions you authorized. A mismatch is an opportunity to revise the words before anyone acts on them.

A change model such as John Kotter’s eight-step approach can give a team a broader view of the people, direction and sustained effort a transition needs. It will not supply missing facts about one appointment. Set aside time after the immediate issue to consider whether this incident exposed a recurring gap in how changes are communicated. If you repeatedly learn of changes from worried employees, ask the person who manages implementation to establish when supervisors and front-line staff will receive updates. A habit of managing your own response can help reveal an organizational condition that no amount of personal composure can fix.

scenario: A change will start a month earlier than expected. Staff ask whether tomorrow's appointments should be cancelled. A supervisor feels pressure to give an immediate, confident answer.
decision: What would you say in the first few minutes?

choices.label: Give a temporary instruction to hold the slots while the authorized owner confirms the impact.
choices.feedback: Staff can preserve options and know when the question will be settled. Check whether any appointments need action before that time.

choices.label: Ask staff which appointments would be hardest to reinstate, and assign someone to verify those first.
choices.feedback: You use staff knowledge to protect urgent decisions. State who can change a booking so the question does not become an unofficial cancellation.

perspective: A scheduler already heard your surprised remark as permission to cancel and has contacted a resident.
reconsider: What repair does that resident need in addition to the team update?
reflection: Which words or gestures from someone with authority might sound like a decision?
transfer: Draft a thirty-second update. Include one confirmed fact, one action staff can take and a time for the next answer.
followup: Distinguish a decision staff may make now from a question still being checked. Tell them when they will hear back.

title: Practicing empathy when a colleague needs support
objective: Support a distressed colleague while protecting the person they serve
learn: How to listen for what troubled someone, then name who will verify a fact and who will contact the caller

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: An experienced employee comes to a check-in upset after a difficult call. You know the procedure and have three suggestions ready. Before you offer any of them, find out what mattered to the employee. They might be concerned about the caller, about an instruction they could not explain, or about being expected to take another call immediately. An accurate understanding changes what support makes sense.

teaching.title: Give the other person room to correct you
teaching.text:
Pity can put distance between people. Sympathy expresses concern. Empathy takes the further step of trying to understand an experience from the other person’s position. Compassion involves acting with that understanding. To practice empathy, put aside distractions, ask what happened and reflect the part you think matters most. “It sounds as though having no answer to give was the hardest part. Have I understood?” leaves room for a correction.

Suppose the employee says the hardest part was actually overhearing a coworker make light of the caller’s problem. A quick suggestion about handling difficult calls would have missed the issue entirely. Ask what response the employee hopes for. Explain any responsibility you have to act, what information you need and how you will follow up. Make only the promises you can keep. Empathy can make it possible to give difficult feedback or raise a concern plainly because you understand the consequences people are living with.

teaching.title: Let the follow-up show what you heard
teaching.text:
Praise might recognize that the employee navigated a difficult call. More specific recognition could name how their careful explanation helped the person understand the next step. Appreciation can acknowledge the attention the employee gives people on difficult days, including occasions when there is no immediate fix. Choose words you can support from what you observed, and ask whether public or private recognition would be welcome.

At the next check-in, return to the part that mattered. Did the concern receive a response? Has anything changed for the employee or the people calling? If you misunderstood, accept the correction and adjust. You can judge the value of your listening by whether it helped both of you identify the right problem and follow it through.

teaching.title: Hold space for the employee and the service commitment
teaching.text:
A conversation about a hard call may lead to a performance question. Suppose a colleague listened carefully to a resident who was struggling to explain a concern. The colleague then gave a date they could not verify because they wanted to reassure the caller. The care was sincere. The person now expects an answer on a day the agency may be unable to deliver. If a supervisor focuses only on the mistake, the employee may miss the value of listening closely. Focusing only on the good intention leaves the resident relying on an uncertain promise.

Invite the employee to walk through the moment when they chose to give a date. Ask what they understood about the caller’s immediate need and what choices they thought were available. They may have known the limits of their authority but lacked a usable phrase for uncertainty. They may have received contradictory coaching. Or the office may have given front-line staff no dependable way to get an answer. Each explanation changes the next action. Trace the actual need far enough that coaching the employee and repairing the service failure can both happen.

teaching.title: Translate understanding into a responsible response
teaching.text:
Use Coaching Conversations That Help People Grow with a colleague who can play the employee. Try a response that names the impact and leaves room for what you have yet to learn. For example, “The caller left counting on Friday. What did you know about that date when you gave it?” Listen for the employee’s account before proposing words to use next time. Then decide who can verify the date, who will contact the resident and who will make sure the reply gets through. Practicing a more accurate sentence will help the next caller. It cannot repair a promise to the current one.

Return separately to how the difficult encounter affected the employee. Would a few minutes away from the phones help? Is a follow-up with the colleague who made the dismissive remark needed? A servant leadership approach asks what obstruction the supervisor can remove. A coaching approach gives the employee a chance to practice judgment with support. Use both where they fit. Ask at the next check-in whether the adjustment made it easier to do the work and what still needs a decision. That question makes room for an unwelcome answer if the first response fell short.

scenario: After a difficult call an employee appears upset. They spoke carefully to the resident but promised a Friday response without having confirmed it.
decision: How will you support the employee while repairing the service commitment?

choices.label: Ask which part of the call troubled the employee and then establish exactly what the caller was promised.
choices.feedback: Listening may reveal a concern you missed. Agree who will verify the promised date and who will contact the resident.

choices.label: Arrange a colleague to cover the next call and verify the response time while you speak privately with the employee.
choices.feedback: This gives the employee space and gets someone checking the facts. Bring the employee's account into the follow-up before the message goes out.

perspective: The employee says the hardest moment was hearing a coworker dismiss the resident's concern. The promised date was an attempt to reassure the caller.
reconsider: What needs attention in the workplace as well as in the response to the caller?
reflection: What observation led to your first explanation of the employee's distress?
transfer: In a practice replay, give the employee a chance to correct your interpretation and close with a named owner for the resident's follow-up.
followup: Find out what troubled the employee, then identify who will verify the date and contact the caller.

title: Developing yourself through daily work
objective: Use everyday tasks, such as meeting notes, to grow
learn: How to ask others to test your work and check whether disagreement survived the write-up

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A reliable way to find your next learning opportunity is to look at the work other people quietly finish for you. Maybe a colleague always clarifies the decision at the end of a meeting you chair. Maybe someone else catches ambiguity in instructions you write. Their help lets the work proceed, but the repeated pattern also identifies something you could learn. Ask them to show you what they notice.

teaching.title: Get a clear picture of your starting point
teaching.text:
Choose one recurring task that matters to people who rely on your work. Consider a program employee writing guidance for staff who answer questions from residents. Collect a draft you wrote, a revision another person made and a question a staff member still had. Which sentence made the next action clear? Where did readers have to supply information themselves? Ask for input from the people doing the work, including colleagues whose titles give them less authority than yours.

Treat feedback as evidence you can explore. A comment such as “this is too technical” is a starting point. Invite the reader to show you where they stopped and what they thought the sentence meant. If an earlier supervisor raised the same concern, look for a pattern. If you disagree, try the passage with a second reader before dismissing the first. The purpose is to understand the effect of a choice you made.

teaching.title: Practice where someone can see the difference
teaching.text:
Choose a small, observable result. For your next two guidance drafts, ask a colleague unfamiliar with the issue to identify who acts, what they should do and when. Revise and try again. Seek a brief course or a skilled editor’s help if both drafts fail at the same point. New knowledge has a use as soon as it addresses a real difficulty.

At the end of the exercise, identify one technique you can repeat and one question you still have. If unclear instructions have already cost a colleague time, acknowledge the impact and offer a correction. Personal development includes the ability to ask for assistance, receive criticism and repair a mistake. Each is visible in the work people receive from you.

teaching.title: Look for the skill just beyond what you already do well
teaching.text:
An employee who writes exceptionally clear instructions may have more to learn about who gets to influence them. A highly regarded supervisor who welcomes feedback may hear only from people who are comfortable disagreeing in a group. A regular strength can narrow the range of evidence a person sees. To find an appropriate development goal, ask someone who uses your work in a different setting to show you where they have to improvise. Give them a real task and time to work through it. People can often demonstrate a difficulty that would be hard to describe in a survey.

Consider a supervisor who wants meetings to end with clearer decisions. One employee points out that some decisions are clear to everyone in the room yet never reach people who work later shifts. Another says the final note describes a decision as unanimous even when a question was still open. The supervisor’s goal has changed. It now involves accurately communicating what the group settled, preserving unresolved questions and making the result usable across shifts. A more precise goal emerged because people closest to the consequences had a chance to explain them.

teaching.title: Make a self-assessment accountable to the work
teaching.text:
Open Equity leadership self-assessment and growth plan and choose one behavior you can examine in a real work product. For the meeting example, collect two earlier decision notes that can be discussed safely. Ask someone unfamiliar with the discussion to identify what they would do, who can answer a remaining question and whose input is still expected. Invite them to mark their first point of uncertainty. Then ask a participant whether the note accurately preserved disagreement. These two tests tell you different things about your present skill.

Choose a coach or peer observer for the next attempt. Agree on what you want them to watch, such as whose closing account became the official account. Give them permission to tell you that a favored technique made the problem worse. A leader practicing personal accountability can acknowledge what they learned and correct the record if necessary. Several weeks later, have a colleague from a different shift use a subsequent note. A change that still works when your coach is absent gives you stronger evidence of learning. It also helps you identify whether the next issue belongs in your own development plan or in the way the team distributes decisions.

scenario: Your meeting notes reach several shifts. Colleagues routinely interpret the notes for people who were absent. You want to develop your ability to close a decision clearly.
decision: How would you test the next set of notes?

choices.label: Ask someone on a different shift to identify who acts, when and which decision is still open.
choices.feedback: A reader can expose missing instructions that participants supplied from memory. Accuracy also needs checking by someone who was there.

choices.label: Ask one participant to mark which conclusions the group reached and which remained disputed.
choices.feedback: You can learn whether disagreement survived the write-up. A correct record can still be difficult for another shift to use.

perspective: An evening worker can identify the task but believes the vote was unanimous. A meeting participant says an objection was left for the next discussion.
reconsider: Which sentence would you revise to make both the action and uncertainty legible?
reflection: How do you tell whether a colleague is repairing your communication for you?
transfer: Test the next two sets of fictional notes with an absent reader and a participant. Name the change you would carry forward.
followup: Ask someone on another shift to use the notes and a participant to check whether disagreement survived the write-up.

title: Emotional intelligence in everyday interactions
objective: Respond well when someone corrects you in public; keep it safe for staff to raise errors
learn: How to check a challenged fact without defensiveness, and how a leader's response teaches staff whether speaking up is safe

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: At a review meeting, a colleague taps her pen while another person explains a difficult service decision. Someone interprets the tapping as impatience. The colleague may be concentrating, may be uncomfortable or may actually want the meeting to move along. The sound is observable. Its meaning is uncertain. Emotional intelligence includes knowing what you are feeling, noticing what you communicate and giving other people a fair chance to explain themselves.

teaching.title: Read your own signals first
teaching.text:
Before interpreting someone else’s reaction, pay attention to your own. A tight jaw, a raised voice or a rush to interrupt may alert you to something you care about. Disappointment may tell you that a hoped-for improvement has stalled. Frustration may point to a barrier you have met repeatedly. The feeling is information you can use to choose your next words. It gives you limited evidence about another person’s intention.

In the meeting, the person presenting might say, “I’m losing my place, and I want to make sure I explain the decision clearly. Is there a part you want me to slow down for?” If a private conversation would better serve the colleague, save it for later. A supervisor can also change the meeting design by circulating the issue in advance or giving people time to write questions. Eye contact, physical stillness and immediate spoken responses are unreliable tests of attention.

teaching.title: Handle an impact you did not intend
teaching.text:
Imagine you looked at the clock repeatedly as a colleague described an error that affected a resident. They later say they felt rushed. You can explain that you were tracking an upcoming deadline after you acknowledge what they experienced. Ask which issue went unheard and arrange time to address it. Next time, tell the speaker how much time you have and offer another time if the subject needs it.

Invite that kind of feedback from more than the people who already feel at ease with you. If a colleague asks about your tone, they have provided information that would otherwise be hard to get. Give the relationship room for occasional misunderstandings and enough attention to repair repeated ones. People express concern and respect in different ways, and curiosity is a practical way to learn which signs matter in this relationship.

teaching.title: Explore how two people can misread each other
teaching.text:
In an emotionally charged conversation, both people are interpreting what they see. A staff member may concentrate by looking away while a supervisor takes steady eye contact as a sign of engagement. The supervisor’s effort to catch the employee’s eye may feel intrusive. Each person’s adjustment can deepen the misunderstanding. Identity, past experience, communication access and the immediate situation can all matter. Nobody in the room can determine which explanation fits by looking at the other person. Start with the small piece you can state accurately and ask what would make the discussion easier.

A manager can make the conversation safer by describing their own need first. “I have to check the dates against the written sequence. Would it work if we read it separately and then compare where we got stuck?” This gives the employee a practical choice. It also lets the manager find out whether their way of explaining the work contributed to the problem. Where a specific behavior caused harm, describe the behavior and its effect directly. Guessing at someone’s emotional state is a poor substitute for addressing what happened.

teaching.title: Practice the response from both positions
teaching.text:
In Emotional Intelligence in Conversations, Teams, and Leadership, approach the lesson once as the person offering feedback and again as the person receiving it. Imagine that a new analyst challenges a manager’s figures during a public presentation. The manager experiences embarrassment and hears disrespect. The analyst saw an error that affected the conclusion and believed a correction had to happen before the discussion moved on. Have each describe what they observed, what they inferred and what they needed in that moment. Give each a way to revise their account after hearing the other.

A supervisor has an extra responsibility here. If staff learn that correcting an error publicly brings personal criticism later, the next person may stay quiet while a mistake affects a decision. The supervisor could say, “I want errors raised when they could change what we decide. I also want us to make clear which number is in question so I can check it.” Agree on a way to flag an issue during a meeting and a way to correct the public record afterward. Later, ask whether staff can actually use the arrangement when the person presenting is senior. Learning to recognize emotion can improve a specific decision and the conditions for the person who needs to challenge the next one.

scenario: A junior analyst says a figure in a manager's presentation uses the wrong reporting period. The meeting has twelve minutes left, and the figure would influence a staffing decision.
decision: How should the manager respond in the room?

choices.label: Pause the decision and ask the analyst to identify the period and source for the disputed figure.
choices.feedback: People see the concern taken seriously. Avoid putting the sole burden of proving the error on the person who raised it.

choices.label: Proceed with unaffected items and have two colleagues check the figures before the staffing decision resumes.
choices.feedback: The meeting can move forward and the decision stays reversible. Explain to everyone when the correction will be heard.

perspective: The analyst says they hesitated because the last public correction was described as disrespectful. The manager remembers being embarrassed, not intending to discourage anyone.
reconsider: How would you make the next correction safe to raise and verify that the invitation is credible?
reflection: Which part of the reaction was about the factual risk, and which part was about status?
transfer: Write the public correction you would make if the analyst is right. Include how the team will handle the next time.
followup: Look for an answer that keeps staff able to raise consequential errors, even when a more senior person is speaking.
