title: Help your team work through a change
theme: Teams and the work they carry
objective: Give staff the instructions they need when a new process meets a real case
learn: How to walk urgent and routine cases through a new route and name who handles exceptions when the usual contact is away

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A supervisor learns that two teams will begin using one route for service questions. The reason makes sense to leadership. An employee answering a county partner’s call has more immediate questions. Can I still contact the specialist I know? Who handles an urgent issue? Will my role change? Write the first announcement with that employee’s next working day in mind. A leader’s job continues through the first time the new route fails to work as expected.

teaching.title: Make it possible to distinguish a decision from an open question
teaching.text:
Before the announcement, ask a supervisor from an affected shift to read it and walk through a typical inquiry. Identify the reason for the change, the first day it applies, the decisions staff still make and where current instructions will live. Put a name or role beside each outstanding question. If a staffing question is unresolved or details cannot yet be shared, say what you are authorized to say, who can provide an update and when staff will hear from you again.

Equip the people who will answer questions when you are away. A shift lead needs the same current information as a manager. Someone answering calls needs a way to reach help while a person is waiting. Walk through what will happen with inquiries that arrive before the start date and remain open afterward. This often brings a gap into view before anyone has to improvise with a caller.

teaching.title: Stay available through the first attempts
teaching.text:
On the first day, try the new route yourself with a practice example. If staff need access they do not have, arrange it or identify who can. Invite people to raise questions in a huddle or privately afterward. Return to the same questions on later shifts. Repetition may mean the instructions were difficult to apply or missed the people who needed them.

During the following week, ask colleagues to bring an instance where the change worked and one where it introduced delay. Use the evidence to adjust the instructions, clarify ownership or raise a decision beyond your authority. Record the answer in the shared guidance so that an employee returning from leave has the same chance to succeed as someone who heard every announcement.

A staff member asking whether a new system will eliminate positions is raising a different question from how to use the system. Explain what has been decided about roles, what remains undecided and who can provide an authorized answer. Before announcing the change, rehearse that question with the managers who will hear it on other shifts so staff receive consistent information.

teaching.title: Make uncertainty usable on a busy shift
teaching.text:
A staff member receiving a referral through the new route has a person on the line, a case that needs attention today and a message saying the specialist is unavailable. “We will communicate as we learn more” gives the staff member little to work with. Identify the next decision they can safely make, where they can seek an exception and what to tell the person waiting. If the process owner has yet to decide how urgent referrals will be handled, bring that gap to the owner before treating it as a communications problem. Better wording cannot assign authority.

Draw a short timeline for the change. On it, place the known effective date, the next decision, the next opportunity for staff to comment and the date the team will revisit exceptions. If the date of a decision is uncertain, name when the owner expects to give an update. Consider what a missed update would cost. A partner might continue referring people to an old address or commit to a turnaround time the new team cannot meet. Communicate first where the uncertainty could have a consequence for someone outside the organization.

teaching.title: Give people a reason to speak about what is failing
teaching.text:
In Trust during uncertainty and change, learners examine the meanings people can attach to speaking before they are certain. Some staff will offer an emerging concern. Others may wait until they can demonstrate it. Use that difference to design a low-risk rehearsal. Give employees a sample referral, let each shift try the instructions independently and ask where they had to improvise. This produces evidence from the process and leaves people free to explain what prompted a choice.

Adaptive leadership is useful while the team is discovering how a change affects different work. A directive decision can be necessary when delays leave a person without a responsible contact. Explain why the approach changed and when staff can shape it again. For example, a supervisor can temporarily designate a backup for urgent referrals while asking both teams to propose a sustainable arrangement. People should know which part is an immediate safety or continuity decision and which part remains open to design.

One week into use, compare two routes through the service. Did a routine inquiry arrive sooner? Did a complex inquiry move between offices an extra time? A shorter average can coexist with a worse experience for people who need an exception. Bring both results to the change owner and state what adjustment you recommend, whose work it would change and which participants can tell whether it helped.

scenario: Two units will use one route for incoming inquiries. A county partner calls during the first week. The usual specialist is away and the inquiry is urgent.
decision: What guidance should staff receive before using the new route?

choices.label: Walk an urgent inquiry and a routine one through the new process with the receiving team.
choices.feedback: Different routes may require different authority. Name the person who can accept an exception and the next step for the partner.

choices.label: Start with a temporary duty contact and review every exception after the first shift.
choices.feedback: Coverage is clear for today. Give staff a way to report repeated problems so temporary cover does not become a permanent workaround.

perspective: The receiving team can log the inquiry but cannot make the urgent decision. The partner believed a logged inquiry meant someone was acting.
reconsider: What wording and handoff would give the partner a dependable expectation?
reflection: When did you last confuse a completed transmission with an accepted responsibility?
transfer: In a fictional second week, test the route when the duty contact is absent. Revise the first point where ownership breaks down.
followup: Walk an urgent inquiry and a routine one through the new route. Name who handles exceptions when the usual contact is away.

title: Onboard employees through their first year
objective: Help a new employee learn who decides what
learn: How to use a practice inquiry so a new hire can find current guidance, the approver and the exceptions

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A new employee may know Minnesota human services well and still have no way to know which colleague owns a decision in this office. A quiet first week tells a supervisor very little. The questions a person will need to ask often arise only after they have tried the work, seen an exception or had to explain a decision to somebody else. Build those occasions into onboarding and give the employee someone they can reach each time.

teaching.title: Separate what a person needs today from what they can learn through practice
teaching.text:
Before the first day, choose a peer who can demonstrate everyday routines and explain where to find current instructions. Give the peer time to do it. The supervisor retains responsibility for priorities, expectations and feedback. Explain those roles to the employee so they can decide whom to approach with a simple question or a concern they want to discuss privately.

For a person learning to respond to inquiries, start with the equipment, access, privacy guidance and support needed to handle the first practice task. Invite them to observe a colleague explaining the route for a difficult question. Next, have them use an invented example and talk through the reasoning with the peer. Listen for where they had enough information to proceed and where they guessed. That distinction tells the supervisor what to clarify before assigning independent work.

teaching.title: Revisit the job as new situations arise
teaching.text:
Consider short check-ins near the end of each day during the first weeks. Shift to weekly or every other week as the employee becomes more comfortable, then revisit at wider intervals through the first year. Adapt the schedule to the role, work pattern and person’s preference. A calendar entry for a busy supervisor is more dependable than an invitation to stop by whenever a question comes up.

Ask at different points what has become easier, which responsibility they have yet to try and whose work they depend on but have never seen. A six-month conversation may reveal a skill gap the first month could not expose. At the first anniversary, ask which unwritten expectation they had to discover for themselves. Improve the next employee’s introduction while the experience is still fresh.

teaching.title: Teach the rules people usually learn by having an insider
teaching.text:
A new employee can complete every orientation session and still be unable to find out whether a draft letter is ready to go to a county partner. Separate the written approval process from the local practices that people have picked up informally. Ask experienced staff to describe the last letter they sent, including which questions went to a specialist and which they resolved themselves. If two experienced employees give different instructions, give the new employee one accountable contact while the supervisor resolves the difference. Requiring a newcomer to choose which senior worker to believe transfers a leadership problem to the person with least authority.

Give the employee a realistic first task with a safe opportunity to revise. A draft answer to a routine, fictional partner inquiry can reveal a great deal. Can the employee locate the current guidance, explain it in ordinary language and recognize when it would be inappropriate to speculate? The supervisor can model the reasoning once, then let the learner try it on a different example. Explain where practice ends and what must happen before anything is sent externally. Early correction is useful when it prepares the employee to make a sound decision independently.

teaching.title: Build access and relationships into the work itself
teaching.text:
The course Inclusive onboarding for new employees includes lessons on making access and support easy to request and explaining work that newcomers would otherwise have to guess at. Use these lessons to review the first week from the employee’s side. Can they read the materials before a session, find the person who can address a login or access barrier, and join a meeting on the same terms as colleagues? Give a contact and usable alternatives without requiring a personal account in front of the team. Confirm arrangements privately with the appropriate people.

A peer buddy can explain informal routines and make introductions. The supervisor retains responsibility for priorities, assignment expectations and feedback. Coaching fits when the employee is learning how to reason through an exception. Delegation becomes useful once the employee knows what they can decide, who is available for support and which decisions still need review. If the employee brings a question back, examine what they already worked out before deciding that they need the task taken away.

Before closing the first year, invite the employee to identify one piece of knowledge they had to acquire by chance. With their agreement, make it easier for the next hire to find. Ask someone new to the process to try the revised instruction. That small check helps turn individual success into an improvement future colleagues can actually use.

scenario: A new hire has completed orientation. They draft an answer for a county partner and cannot tell whether they may send it or need a reviewer.
decision: How would you teach the next decision safely?

choices.label: Model a routine response, then give the new hire a fictional variation to route and explain.
choices.feedback: You can hear their reasoning and identify whether they know the approval boundary. Include an exception where the routine route would be unsafe.

choices.label: Give them a short map of who owns the answer and ask them to walk an example through it.
choices.feedback: A map can support independent work between meetings. Check whether names and backups are still accurate on the new hire's shift.

perspective: The new hire can name the usual reviewer but cannot find anyone authorized after the reviewer leaves for the day.
reconsider: What would you add to the welcome plan, and how would you see if it works?
reflection: What does finishing orientation establish about readiness to make a particular decision?
transfer: Set a first-month check using one routine question, one exception, and one absent supervisor. Identify the available support for each.
followup: Use a fictional inquiry to test whether they can find current guidance, identify the approver, and recognize an exception.

title: Give feedback that changes the next attempt
objective: Give feedback tied to one specific moment; help someone practice the next attempt
learn: How to recognize what worked, name one change, and rehearse a closing that tells the caller who acts next

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: In a practice call, an employee explains the available service routes accurately, pauses to let the caller choose and ends without checking whether the caller knows whom to contact. A supervisor listening to the exchange has something specific to recognize and a specific point to coach. Describing what happened gives the employee a chance to build on the parts that worked and decide what to try on the next call.

teaching.title: Put the employee’s account beside your observation
teaching.text:
Ask which part of the call they think went well and where they had to make a judgment. Then share one observation at a time. For example, “You gave the caller time to select a route. I heard them ask twice who would call next. How did you understand that question?” Listen for information you did not have. The employee may have expected a colleague to confirm the contact, or the instructions may leave that responsibility unclear.

Make the standard visible. If callers should leave the conversation able to identify the next step, discuss what an employee could say to make that possible. One option is to describe who will contact whom and invite the caller to identify anything still uncertain. Ask the employee how they would phrase it in a way that sounds natural. Give them time to try the closing aloud and revise it.

teaching.title: Return to the work and record the progress
teaching.text:
Agree on the next opportunity to observe and what both people will look for. If the employee needs an updated contact list or training on an unfamiliar route, arrange that support. At follow-up, ask how the revised closing worked across different calls. Look for the quality of the explanation and the caller’s chance to ask another question. A faster call alone would tell you little about either.

Document the example, agreed expectation, assistance and follow-up under the applicable performance process. Record successes with the same specificity as difficulties. An employee seeking a later coaching assignment deserves a record of how they helped callers make sense of a complex choice. When a concern persists or conduct may require a formal response, consult human resources about the next step.

teaching.title: Notice what a performance judgment is based on
teaching.text:
In the practice call, the employee identified the available services and invited the caller to choose. The next issue is whether the caller knows what to do with that choice. A supervisor who says “be more confident with callers” has moved from an observable ending to an assessment of the speaker. Confidence can sound different across people and contexts. It is also a poor substitute for the information a caller needed. Ask the employee to try one additional closing sentence and then let a colleague playing the caller explain what they would do next. That exchange provides usable evidence of the employee’s skill.

Apply the same discipline to praise. “That was excellent” can leave an employee guessing which part to repeat. “When you gave the caller time to compare the options, they asked about travel time and chose the one they could reach” identifies a skill and a consequence. Give the employee a chance to correct your interpretation. Perhaps the caller had already chosen, and the pause allowed them to ask a different question. Feedback becomes more accurate when both people can contribute observations.

teaching.title: Give the employee room to correct the supervisor
teaching.text:
Feedback across power differences examines what changes when one participant assigns work or evaluates the other. A person who says little may be taking time to think, weighing the cost of disagreement or simply agreeing. The supervisor has an opportunity to make a correction possible without demanding that the employee perform confidence or disclose personal experiences. “Which part of the call did I hear differently from you?” is easier to answer when followed by time to listen and a clear explanation of how any notes will be used.

Rehearse a harder variation. The caller needed an interpreter, and the call lasted longer than a supervisor expected. A feedback conversation that begins with call duration can send the unintended message that arranging access counts against performance. Examine what the employee was expected to accomplish, what work was within their authority and which part of the delay they could influence. If a system step needs changing, the supervisor can take responsibility for raising it while still coaching a specific communication skill.

Use coaching for the next attempt and clear expectations where the person needs to know how their work will be assessed. If the conversation concerns a continuing performance problem, follow the appropriate supervisory and human resources guidance. Keep practice examples separate from any actual personnel record. End with a concrete arrangement for observing the new skill, including who will give feedback, which part of the interaction they will look for and when the employee can respond.

scenario: A worker gives a resident a clear explanation and pauses to let them respond. The resident asks twice who will make the next call.
decision: Which feedback will help the worker improve the next attempt?

choices.label: Name the helpful pause and rehearse two possible closings with a colleague playing the caller.
choices.feedback: Specific recognition preserves something effective. Let the caller explain what each closing led them to expect.

choices.label: Ask the worker what they intended the resident to do and replay the final exchange together.
choices.feedback: You may discover an unclear handoff rather than a weakness in delivery. Name what the employee can change and what the supervisor must resolve.

perspective: The employee says they do not know when the receiving unit accepts callbacks. A confident closing would require inventing a time.
reconsider: How would you make the closing useful while the receiving unit checks ownership?
reflection: How can feedback hold both the person's skill and a gap in the work system in view?
transfer: Write a closing that names the current owner, the next update and what the resident can do if that update does not arrive.
followup: Recognize the employee’s useful pause and rehearse a closing that lets the caller identify who acts next.

title: Build psychological safety into daily work
objective: Respond to a concern so the person who raised it is glad they did
learn: How to act on a concern, assign the follow-up, and tell the person what happened as a result

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A new employee discovers that yesterday’s outgoing letter gives two different phone numbers. They can quietly correct the copy on their desk, or they can tell their supervisor that other people may already have received it. Psychological safety affects whether someone can bring that second piece of information forward when doing so may expose a mistake or invite an uncomfortable question. The supervisor’s first response will be visible to more people than the one who spoke.

teaching.title: Respond in a way that protects the person and the work
teaching.text:
Thank the employee for bringing the discrepancy forward. Ask which version they saw, where it came from and whether people using it may need help. Make the immediate correction or involve someone who can. Use the appropriate process if there are privacy or other reporting concerns. Take responsibility for getting the issue to the right place. When it is possible to share an update, tell the employee what happened and acknowledge their contribution.

Later, examine how the discrepancy entered circulation and why someone caught it only after the letter went out. If you approved an earlier version, acknowledge your own part and identify what you will change. Invite people who handle the letters to suggest a way to catch the next mismatch. Deal privately and fairly with any individual performance issue that emerges. Public humiliation gives everyone who witnessed it a reason to stay silent next time.

teaching.title: Look at the work people are being asked to accept
teaching.text:
Give a new assignment with time to ask questions, a realistic deadline, a named person for backup and room to say what existing work it will displace. A person learning a new task may need a colleague present for the first attempt. A person covering two jobs may need one priority removed. A supervisor who adjusts the assignment provides concrete evidence that raising a concern can change what happens.

Watch what happens after the invitation for questions. Do people identify problems early? Does someone who is away from the main office have the same route to assistance? Does the team know who covers planned time off? Consistent answers make speaking and listening easier even when the issue is serious.

teaching.title: Learn what happened after somebody spoke
teaching.text:
A quick correction to the phone number solves the problem for the next reader. It says little about what happened to the residents who received the earlier letter or the colleague who raised the discrepancy. An ethical response gives both matters an owner. Who can determine how widely the letter was distributed and decide what communication is appropriate? Who will tell the reporting employee what the unit learned? If either question remains unassigned, people who saw the error may conclude that speaking up changes a document on one desk and little else.

The course Accountability without blame: tracking equity commitments provides a way to select evidence that fits a promise. Apply it to the supervisor’s public commitment to correct conflicting contact instructions. A new version in the shared folder establishes that the text was changed. A check of the outgoing print queue establishes whether the old version can still be sent. A call placed through the revised number establishes that someone can reach the intended destination on that occasion. Choose the test that matches the promise, identify what remains uncertain and give staff enough context to see why another check is necessary.

teaching.title: Make it safe to disagree with the person investigating the error
teaching.text:
Suppose an employee points out that the wrong number came from a previously approved template. The supervisor who approved it can reduce the cost of speaking by naming their own decision and inviting evidence of other places the number appears. They can also make it clear what staff should do if they discover an error outside their area of authority. In some situations a formal reporting route is appropriate. A supervisor can explain that route and make the necessary referral without sharing personal information in a team debrief.

Psychological safety shows up before an error as well as afterward. Review one assignment that depends on a single expert. Who can question an unrealistic deadline? Who will cover the task when the expert takes leave? A person consistently praised for rescuing work may be carrying a workload that keeps everyone else from learning. Invite them to name one decision a colleague could make with support. Provide the colleague with practice time, access to the right guidance and a clear point at which to seek help.

Watch for a change you can actually interpret. More early questions after staff receive a dependable response can reflect better visibility into existing difficulties. Fewer reports may mean improvement, silence or less opportunity to observe the work. Pair the number of reports with examples of what the team corrected and what happened the next time someone raised a concern.

scenario: A new colleague finds two contact numbers in a letter already mailed. They raise it during the morning huddle and then go quiet.
decision: How will you respond in a way that makes future concerns easier to raise?

choices.label: Thank the colleague for the specific observation, assign a check of both numbers, and agree when the team will hear back.
choices.feedback: The group sees a concern leading to action. Decide separately who will consider the impact on people who already received the letter.

choices.label: Ask privately what else the colleague saw and arrange immediate coverage while the contact details are checked.
choices.feedback: A private conversation can surface uncertainty. The team still needs a public update on the correction and how to report further problems.

perspective: The new colleague thought they might be blamed for slowing the mailing. Several coworkers knew about the numbers but believed the template was fixed.
reconsider: What would you tell the full team once the facts are checked? What would you ask beyond whether people felt heard?
reflection: What happened the last time someone questioned a settled instruction in your fictional team?
transfer: In a replay, set a time to report what the concern changed and name how someone on another shift can flag the next error.
followup: Assign someone to check the effect on earlier recipients and tell the employee what happened after they raised it.

title: Help a team think strategically
objective: Lead a team to test options before committing staff to one
learn: How to compare repeat calls with processing times and check who waits longer if staff are moved

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A program team sees more calls asking for the status of service inquiries and proposes assigning another employee to answer the phone. Before anyone moves staff, ask the group to work through the decision together. Strategic thinking involves observing what is happening, analyzing the choices, drawing and testing inferences, hearing other people’s reasoning and solving the problem that the evidence supports. Each of those skills can be practiced in an ordinary team meeting.

teaching.title: Work through a decision with evidence in view
teaching.text:
Begin with an observation the team could verify. How many people called, over what period, and about which stage of the process? Count repeat contacts separately from distinct inquiries if the available records permit it. An increase in calls could reflect a longer wait, an unexpected notice or a contact number that now sends more people to this team. Ask someone to identify which of these explanations the existing information can distinguish.

Next, look at how the facts constrain a choice. A staff transfer might shorten time on hold but lengthen the queue that prompted the calls. A clearer update might help someone who is waiting for a routine response but do little for someone with an urgent need. Invite the staff handling the inquiries and those receiving the transfers to explain what each option would change during a typical shift. Ask about an earlier attempt and which conditions have changed since then.

teaching.title: Make the reasoning available to the next team
teaching.text:
Choose a small action that can teach the group something. The team could try a clearer status message for one category of inquiries and compare the pattern of follow-up contacts over a defined period. Agree in advance on who can authorize the change, what would justify expanding it and what would prompt the team to stop. A promising result may still depend on time of year or on who received the new message.

Keep the decision, assumptions, observations and follow-up date together in the appropriate work records. Follow the agency’s guidance for retaining records and handling personal information. When another unit sees a similar pattern, it can examine the reasoning, identify what transfers to its situation and avoid repeating a choice whose conditions no longer hold.

teaching.title: Make two explanations compete for the same evidence
teaching.text:
For the team facing an increase in status calls, consider two plausible explanations. Under the first, requests are moving through the program more slowly. Under the second, requests move at the usual pace, but people have stopped receiving an acknowledgment with a reliable estimate of the next contact. Both explanations fit a full phone queue. They would lead the team to spend scarce staffing time differently. Name one observation you would expect under each. Then look for the information that would help the team distinguish the two.

Use Equity dashboards: from display to decisions to practice reading what a measure includes. A count of completed calls tells you about callers who got through. It cannot tell you how many people tried repeatedly and abandoned the call, or who used a trusted partner instead. A high completion rate in a small category can be especially hard to interpret. Before comparing groups, establish the time period, the denominator and how much information is missing. Work through the authorized data channels and give the decision maker only the detail the decision calls for.

teaching.title: Decide what to do while several explanations remain plausible
teaching.text:
A manager could assign another worker to phones for a short period to protect access while a second team examines acknowledgments. Give the arrangement an explicit review date and a question worth answering. Did repeat status calls drop after people began receiving clearer information? Did adding phone capacity shorten waits but move a backlog to another part of the process? Identify whose experience can illuminate each measure. A partner organization may hear from people who never reach the team; a front-line worker can show what a person sees when their request enters the system.

Strategic perspective develops when a leader can explain both an immediate action and how it affects other parts of the organization. Participative leadership brings in knowledge that a central dashboard cannot provide. Procedural discipline keeps the group’s record of its decision usable after a staff change. Save the reasons for the choice, including the evidence that would lead the team to reverse or modify it, in an appropriate shared location. A colleague taking over the pilot should be able to see why another explanation was set aside.

Try applying the same sequence to a favorable result. If requests are completed faster, examine whether people understand the outcome and can reach someone about a mistake. A decision can improve speed while creating new work elsewhere. Leaders who go looking for that possibility are teaching colleagues a method they can use again.

scenario: Status calls are rising while application processing is already stretched. You have one worker available for reassignment. A revised acknowledgment may also help residents know when to expect a response.
decision: Will you move the worker, change the acknowledgment first, or test a combination?

choices.label: Temporarily shift coverage to the busiest call window and set a decision date for returning it.
choices.feedback: Residents can reach a person sooner. Track whether the move lengthens the queue that generated the calls in the first place.

choices.label: Test a clearer acknowledgment with a small group while keeping processing coverage steady.
choices.feedback: You can learn which questions wording will resolve. Urgent callers may still need immediate access to someone who can act.

perspective: Staff who answer the phone say some residents know the expected date and are calling because it has already passed.
reconsider: Which callers need a better notice, and which need a service decision?
reflection: What could improve on one dashboard while people wait longer in practice?
transfer: Draw the expected effect of each option on both queues. Write one finding that would make you reverse the decision.
followup: Compare repeat calls with processing times and check who waits longer if a worker moves.

title: Use participation where people can shape a decision
objective: Invite participation only where people can truly change the outcome
learn: How to state what partners can choose, include people on fixed shifts, and show which concern changed the result

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A manager wants to improve how community partners reach a program team. They can invite feedback on the current contact route, ask partners to help design alternatives or ask them to choose among options. These invitations give people different degrees of influence. Explain which one you are making before anyone spends an evening preparing comments. People can contribute to a decision they disagree with when they understand the question, their role and how the final choice was made.

teaching.title: Decide whose experience the team needs
teaching.text:
Start with the actual choice and the limits around it. For example, the program may have to use existing staffing but may be able to change when callbacks are offered. Identify who will gain or lose access under different schedules. Include people who handle the calls, partners who make referrals and people who try to use the route without a partner. Ask how they would like to take part. One advisory member cannot describe every user’s experience.

Design participation around the question. A small workshop can compare alternatives and expose tradeoffs. Individual interviews may reveal problems someone would hesitate to raise in front of a supervisor. A short written response can give people time to check an idea with others. Arrange accessible formats and communication supports, and allow time for replies. An experienced facilitator can help when authority, competing interests or a difficult history make a group discussion hard to run fairly.

teaching.title: Show what happened to the contributions
teaching.text:
Suppose people on a fixed work schedule say that a broadly worded promise of a daytime callback makes it hard to answer. Ask what a more usable arrangement would require. Test any proposed time window with the staff who must cover it and the people who would receive the call. Give both groups a chance to identify a difficulty the other may not have seen.

When the manager makes the decision, report which suggestions changed it, which could not be adopted and why. Name a point when people can report how the new arrangement works in practice. A person who helped design it should be able to recognize where their experience entered the decision and who owns the next adjustment.

teaching.title: Choose a way of working that fits the public decision
teaching.text:
A short survey, a discussion with a facilitator and a joint design session invite very different contributions. If the team needs to know which of three existing contact routes partners can actually use, a short comparison followed by interviews may be sufficient. If none of the three routes works for many people, a vote among them locks the group into an inadequate choice. Invite people to describe a recent attempt and show where it broke down. That evidence can help the team develop another option before asking anyone to choose.

Meaningful community engagement for leaders includes practice in identifying who is absent and in hearing disagreement without losing its meaning. Apply it before invitations go out. Write a paragraph explaining which parts of a service decision can still change and who will make the choice. Read it as a person who has missed three callbacks, a family member supporting someone who prefers to speak for themselves, and a program worker who will maintain the new arrangement. Which of those people would recognize a reason to take part? Which might need a different time, format or contact route? Confirm these needs with participants.

teaching.title: Give a facilitator a question with an honest answer
teaching.text:
Human-centered design can help a group examine the steps a person takes and try an alternative. Appreciative inquiry can surface a practice that already succeeds under difficult conditions. A consensus workshop can help participants organize possibilities and discover common ground. Choose the method based on the decision, the people affected and the authority they have been given. If the sponsor will make the final choice, explain the grounds on which they will weigh competing needs. A capable facilitator can prevent one voice from dominating a meeting. They cannot give a group decision authority that the sponsor has withheld.

Consider a partner who objects to the proposed callback arrangement because it would exclude people who cannot take private calls during a shift. A participant may disagree and value a predictable appointment. Preserve the reason for both positions in the record. “Participants preferred appointments” would omit evidence needed to consider a fallback contact method. Bring the record back in a form participants can correct, and give the person who decides time to respond before launch.

When a decision is unpopular, a supervisor can exercise participative leadership by explaining whose evidence changed the design and which constraint prevailed. Acknowledge the concern that remains unresolved and who can revisit it. Treat the quality of influence as an outcome. People should be able to recognize their contribution in the reasoning even when their preferred option was set aside.

scenario: Partners can influence evening callback hours within current staffing. One proposed meeting time excludes people working fixed shifts. The service location and budget have already been decided.
decision: What part of the schedule will partners help choose and how will they influence it?

choices.label: Offer two feasible schedules and invite an alternative within the same staffing limit.
choices.feedback: People can compare concrete options. Explain who will decide when two groups need the same scarce window.

choices.label: Ask partners to explain when a callback can actually be received, then build options with them.
choices.feedback: The group can tell you about barriers you missed. Give people more than one way to contribute before the staffing deadline.

perspective: A partner says the evening window works for people who have a private phone. Another person needs a planned time at a shared phone.
reconsider: How would you handle these different needs and report the remaining trade-off?
reflection: Which word in your invitation might imply that a fixed decision is still open?
transfer: Write the invitation and a short response to one suggestion the service cannot adopt. Give the reason and the next opportunity to revisit it.
followup: Show which partner concern changed the schedule and who will revisit a conflict the group could not settle.

title: Use authority in service of others
objective: Remove an obstacle so a resident can take part in the way they choose
learn: How to ask before committing the team, and how to leave the resident in control of how they participate

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A leadership title changes what you can authorize, whose call is returned and which concerns reach a director. Servant leadership asks how you use that access on behalf of the people doing and receiving the work. Minnesota’s 2019 creation of the One Minnesota Council on Inclusion and Equity gave public expression to a commitment to inclusion. A supervisor can give that commitment practical meaning in a specific decision and accept responsibility for the result.

teaching.title: Let the people who experience a barrier help define it
teaching.text:
Imagine a notice has gone out announcing community listening sessions, and an interested resident asks how to participate from home. The department already has a busy calendar of in-person sessions. Before calling the request a scheduling problem, ask the resident what participation would require and whether they would like to hear about alternatives. Ask the staff organizing the sessions which constraints they can address and which require a manager’s decision.

A supervisor can use their position to secure staff time, raise an access need with the event owner or ask for a revised plan. Let the colleagues who understand the logistics shape the options and let the resident decide whether an option is useful to them. If a change will take time, identify who can answer questions in the meantime. Taking over every conversation can leave everyone dependent on the supervisor the next time a barrier appears.

teaching.title: Account publicly for the decisions within your control
teaching.text:
If you approved the original schedule, acknowledge that decision and the participation it made difficult. Explain what you changed, who will follow up and how people will hear whether the arrangement worked. An apology carries weight when the person can see the repair. Protect a resident’s privacy when describing a lesson to colleagues. A team can learn from the gap without identifying the person who first pointed it out.

Carry what you learned into the next planning discussion. Ask staff whose experience they still need and whether their usual method of seeking input can reach those people. Keep learning about the communities affected by the team’s work and invite correction when your understanding is incomplete. The responsibility to act on what you learn belongs to you as well as to the people who were willing to teach you.

teaching.title: Serve a person who disagrees with the offer of help
teaching.text:
Imagine a planning session where a staff member and a relative do most of the speaking while the person seeking services uses a communication device. A well-intentioned leader may wish to shorten the meeting by completing their sentences or asking the relative to choose among the options. Start by asking the person how they want to communicate, who they want involved and what would make the discussion workable. Make time for their answer. A person’s decision to involve someone they trust can be an exercise of their authority. A professional decision to substitute someone else’s judgment changes who is directing the conversation.

The application course Centering people with disabilities in decision-making takes the learner through participation arrangements, preparation and support, as well as how to keep someone’s priorities visible when other people assist. Use it to prepare an alternative to a hurried planning session. Offer the questions in advance and arrange a way for the person to contribute privately, with support or over more than one contact when feasible. Confirm with them which words they want recorded and where the team will carry their input. Explain any formal decision or eligibility question that remains with an authorized person.

teaching.title: Spend authority on the obstacle the person cannot remove
teaching.text:
A supervisor might be able to change the meeting schedule, arrange an accessible document or reserve staff time to follow up. The resident cannot fix those agency arrangements by being more assertive. Use your authority to remove a specific obstacle and be clear about the part you cannot approve. If a different area controls the resource, find the responsible contact, obtain permission before sharing personal details where needed and take responsibility for returning with an answer. A promise to advocate carries little value if the person is sent from one contact to the next to find out whether it happened.

Servant leadership and supported decision-making raise an important tension. An energetic leader can make things happen quickly and still crowd out the person whose life the decision concerns. Inclusive leadership helps the group hear what has been overlooked. Ethical leadership helps the supervisor own unintended harm and explain the remedy. Ask a colleague to observe whether staff interrupt, whom they address when the person uses support and whose words appear in the final account. Discuss the observations without making assumptions about anyone’s identity or capacity.

If the person later says the account missed what mattered, reopen the part the team can change and identify the proper route for the rest. A revised record and a real change in how the next conversation proceeds are concrete evidence that the organization received the correction.

interaction: Use authority to remove a barrier
scenario: A resident wants to join a planning conversation from home. The team starts arranging video. The resident has yet to say how they want to take part.
decision: What can you use your authority to change first?

choices.label: Ask the resident which part of participation is difficult, which arrangements have worked, and what they want to control.
choices.feedback: Their answer can change what support is useful. Confirm the practical details before promising a format.

choices.label: Find out which remote and non-digital options the team can support, then offer a genuine choice.
choices.feedback: Concrete options make the decision easier to consider. Leave space for an option the team has not anticipated.

perspective: The resident would like to prepare questions in writing and speak for only part of the meeting. They are worried the team will interpret leaving early as agreement.
reconsider: How would you make their choices about contributing and agreeing clear in the meeting record?
reflection: Where could an offer of help quietly become a decision made for someone?
transfer: Create a one-meeting test of the chosen arrangement and a direct way for the resident to correct the record.
followup: The resident can say whether the option works and still controls how they take part.

title: Influence through example and opportunity
objective: Give credit for an improvement and open the next chance to lead
learn: How to show a team what improved the work and offer a supported leadership chance to the person who found it

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A supervisor asks staff to use plain language when writing to the public, then circulates a memo full of unexplained abbreviations. The team receives two lessons. One is the instruction in the memo. The other is the language that appears to earn approval. Colleagues who lead work without a title face a similar choice every time they prepare an example, respond to a question or recommend someone for an assignment.

teaching.title: Make the practice visible enough to borrow
teaching.text:
Choose a passage that often confuses a reader and show how you would revise it. For example, a sentence might tell people to contact an office about a change in circumstances. Work with the person who knows the procedure to specify which changes matter, who can help and what information someone should have ready. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the process to describe the action the revised sentence calls for. Use their answer to improve the wording.

Share the two versions and explain the decisions behind them. Give credit to the subject expert and the reader who found the remaining ambiguity. A colleague in another unit can now borrow the method for a different notice. They can also see that accuracy still matters when making a sentence easier to read. This is how a small choice can influence work beyond the original team.

teaching.title: Notice who gets the next opportunity
teaching.text:
A person who identified the difficulty may be ready to facilitate the next review. Ask about their interest and what support they want. Recommend them by naming the contribution you observed and the part of the assignment it prepares them to handle. Give them a chance to make decisions and to present the result in their own words. Doing so transfers both responsibility and recognition.

Watch for the habits your own influence may be spreading. If you regularly thank only the person who delivers the final presentation, colleagues may learn to overlook the people who made the work accurate. If you acknowledge a correction made by a newer colleague, other supervisors can see what happens when expertise is recognized across ranks. Invite someone who receives your messages to tell you which example they are actually following.

teaching.title: Make the reasoning visible so a good practice can travel
teaching.text:
A colleague who circulates an excellent plain-language memo has offered a useful example. Colleagues may copy the wording without understanding which features mattered. Make one editorial decision visible. Suppose the first draft said that inquiries would be “routed to the appropriate unit.” The revision says who receives the inquiry, how the person will hear back and what they can do if the expected contact does not occur. Explain how the change answers the reader’s next practical question. A worker can reuse that reasoning in a different program even when the route and the words must change.

In Mentoring and peer learning, the learner works on an example, hears another person’s reasoning and uses a question to make their own revision. Use that sequence with two colleagues. One brings a short public instruction stripped of personal information. The other reads it as a resident trying to act on it and explains where they stopped. The author chooses one revision and says what problem it addresses. A peer’s role is to help make the choice visible. Final approval for public instructions remains with the people who have it.

teaching.title: Notice which practices your influence is rewarding
teaching.text:
The fastest response to a high-profile request may come from the person who routinely works late. If a supervisor repeatedly praises the speed of that response and gives the same person every subsequent assignment, the team may learn that availability outside normal hours is a condition of influence. Others cannot copy that practice on equal terms. Recognize the judgment that improved the response and arrange working time for others to practice it. Credit the colleague who identified a confusing passage, including when someone else presented the finished revision.

A charismatic leader can attract attention to a useful change. Influence is more likely to survive their absence if colleagues understand why the change helped and can make their own decisions. A distributed approach gives the next review to someone with knowledge of the audience and enough authority to carry out the task. Tell them what they may change, who can authorize publication and whom they can consult. If they recommend a different solution, judge it against the person’s ability to use the instruction.

After two teams have tried the method, ask each to bring one example of an improvement and one example where the model did not transfer cleanly. A phrase that works for a scheduled follow-up might confuse someone who has no appointment. Learning where a practice needs adaptation keeps good intentions from spreading a new set of mistakes across the organization.

scenario: A colleague identifies a confusing step in the guidance and tests a revision with the contact center. A manager asks you to present the improvement at an agency meeting.
decision: How will you share both the evidence and the next opportunity?

choices.label: Ask how the colleague wants their contribution credited and offer co-presentation with preparation time.
choices.feedback: This can make their judgment visible. Respect a preference for another form of recognition and cover their regular work.

choices.label: Present the evidence with agreed credit and offer the colleague leadership over the next revision if it fits their goals.
choices.feedback: The role can build capability beyond one presentation. Give it a real decision and name the support it includes.

perspective: The colleague would rather lead the next field test than speak on stage. They want the phone staff who tested the change credited too.
reconsider: How would you redistribute visibility, responsibility and support across the next stage?
reflection: What practice are colleagues likely to copy from the way you use influence here?
transfer: For a fictional next revision, identify who noticed the issue, tested the change, approved it and gets the next choice.
followup: Give credit for the discovery and offer the colleague a supported chance to lead if they want it.

title: Leading through an administrative transition
objective: Tell staff and partners what is settled and what is still open during a transition
learn: How to separate a confirmed change from a pending decision and give everyone one dependable follow-up

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A new administration takes office on a particular day. The work of answering questions, paying vendors and keeping appointments carries on through it. For the staff member who knows which partner to call when a referral goes missing, the most valuable contribution to a transition may be making that knowledge available to someone else. For an incoming director, it may be finding out which quiet arrangements have kept a service working before deciding what to change.

teaching.title: What the outgoing team can leave behind
teaching.text:
Choose one service that people depend on every week. Trace it from the first contact to the last commitment. Identify who can make a decision, who has promised what to whom, and where the next person can find the record. Write down pending choices with their deadlines and the consequences of delay. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the service to use the handoff to answer a real work question. Their first unanswered question tells you what the packet still needs.

During a transition, people can be at different points in letting go of earlier work, finding their footing and committing to what comes next. William Bridges’s transition model gives managers language for those experiences. Set a time for regular updates, even when a decision is pending. A useful update might be, “The schedule for next week stands. The new assignment is awaiting a decision. On Thursday I’ll tell you whether we have one.” Staff can act on each part of that message.

teaching.title: What an incoming leader needs to learn
teaching.text:
The STARS framework, as applied to government by Peter Daly and Michael Watkins, distinguishes starting a new operation, turning around a struggling one, realigning work with new conditions and sustaining a successful effort. A single division may have different assignments in different units. Ask each team what must endure, what has stopped working and what evidence supports that assessment. A call queue that looks slow may include time spent arranging the next contact so a caller can actually use it.

Set one three-month outcome and ask staff and partners how they would recognize progress. Give individual contributors a place to raise a continuity risk or correct an incomplete handoff. When the team tries a change, agree on what would justify keeping, adjusting or reversing it. That gives a new leader room to learn while people can still count on the service.

A new leader can use a Plan–Do–Study–Act cycle on a single handoff. Predict what the new contact arrangement will change, try it with one team, compare the result with the prediction and use what happened to choose the next adjustment. Name both the operational outcome and the experience staff and partners should have while reaching it.

teaching.title: What a supervisor can responsibly say on Monday
teaching.text:
Suppose an email announces a review of outreach contracts. A worker tells a partner that next month’s session has been cancelled. Another worker assures a family that the session will happen as planned. Both heard the same news. One believed that moving early would protect people from disappointment. The other believed that a calm reassurance would keep a relationship intact. Neither had established what the review actually changed. A leader who simply tells the team to “be consistent” leaves them to choose between two equally unsupported answers.

In Leading with values when guidance shifts, work through the lesson on identifying the actual change. Write the sentence you can support from the communication, who issued it, and the part of the service it addresses. Next to it write the question the email leaves open. In the example, determine who can confirm whether the existing session is affected. Give a named worker the follow-up and agree when the partner needs a response. If several programs depend on the session, arrange one update that reaches them all. The continuity decision is now visible to the person who must make it.

teaching.title: Change your approach when the decision changes hands
teaching.text:
Before the decision, a participative approach helps a new manager learn which arrangements people are relying on. A directive response has a different use when a mistaken cancellation is already circulating. The manager can direct staff to correct the inaccurate message, within their authority, while keeping open the question of what happens next month. Trying to reach team consensus about the status of the contract would give participants responsibility for a decision they cannot make.

An outgoing manager has another task. Ask the worker who knows the partner to lead the first update with a successor listening. At the next update reverse their roles. Notice whether the successor knows about the partner’s lead time, preferred contact route and fallback contact without prompting. That is evidence of knowledge transfer. The incoming director can then review a concise record of what staff have promised, what remains open and who owns the next decision. A resident should not have to rebuild the relationship for the agency every time leadership changes.

scenario: A contract review has been announced. A partner tells staff that next month's session is cancelled. An incoming division leader will take over before the contract decision is made.
decision: What should be communicated now and carried through the change in leadership?

choices.label: Confirm what is known with the contract owner and give the partner a time for the next verified update.
choices.feedback: A dependable update can curb rumor without implying a commitment. Name who will provide it if the decision owner changes.

choices.label: Prepare a joint briefing for the outgoing and incoming leads that separates confirmed dates, decisions and open questions.
choices.feedback: The record can prevent inconsistent directions across teams. The partner may need a practical answer sooner than the briefing.

perspective: The partner has to reserve accessible space this week. Waiting for formal confirmation may carry a cost even if the session goes ahead.
reconsider: Which interim choice can an authorized person make, and how will the partner know what it covers?
reflection: Whose deadline was absent from the transition plan?
transfer: Draft a handover note with one confirmed fact, an open decision, its owner, the partner's deadline and a backup contact.
followup: Distinguish the confirmed change from the pending decision. Give staff, partners and the incoming lead one dependable follow-up.

title: Managing a public budget through the year
objective: Decide whether a new commitment fits the budget
learn: How to reconcile money committed, services delivered and invoices paid, then compare who an added service would reach

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A program manager opens the monthly report and sees spending below plan. Has the team saved money, or has an invoice simply not arrived? The answer matters if colleagues are already counting on those dollars for interpretation, staff training or contract work. A manager brings knowledge of what the team has promised. Fiscal colleagues bring knowledge of how commitments appear in the accounts and what the funding permits. A budget conversation needs both.

teaching.title: Read the difference between a plan and a payment
teaching.text:
Ask the fiscal team to walk through the Manager’s Financial Report for your area. Managers with the appropriate access can use SWIFT to obtain it. Pick one line that differs materially from the forecast. Establish what period it covers, what has posted, what is committed and which costs are still expected. Ask about the program calendar. A quarter with little spending can be entirely predictable if a partner bills after a major deliverable.

Consider a unit that expected eight facilitated sessions by June. Six have taken place, the invoice covers four, and two sessions are still scheduled. Three different quantities matter here: sessions planned, sessions delivered and sessions paid for. Before treating the balance as available, reconcile all three with the contract lead. If demand changed, update the forecast and tell the people whose work depends on it.

teaching.title: Decide what the variance calls for
teaching.text:
A vacant position may produce salary savings while colleagues carry extra work. A training balance may mean that nobody can leave the phones during business hours. Ask what the figures mean for staff and for service. The useful decision might be to arrange coverage so employees can attend training, revise an unrealistic estimate, or ask finance whether a one-time expenditure fits the funding terms. A favorable balance alone gives no one authority to commit funds to another purpose.

Choose a review rhythm that matches risk and activity. Record the amount in question, the explanation, the person who will confirm it and the next date to review it. Learn where the program sits in the agency and state budgets so you can explain a proposed expenditure in terms of the public purpose it serves.

teaching.title: Compare who can use the dollars
teaching.text:
A manager has a small one-time balance and two credible proposals. One would cover additional daytime information sessions that an established contractor can start immediately. The other would pay for an evening pilot with interpretation and preparation time for a smaller partner. The first proposal predicts a lower cost per seat. The second may reach people who have been unable to attend. The manager should be able to describe the choice accurately even if the higher-volume option ultimately wins.

Use Equity in rate setting and budget decisions to practice reading a distribution alongside an average. For each proposal, distinguish seats available, people likely to attend, people reached for the first time and people who can use the information afterward. Mark estimates as estimates. The evening partner may know what attendance has looked like elsewhere, yet still need time to learn how this particular group would respond. Compare how each figure was obtained and which costs have been included. A budget that assumes a community organization will coordinate for free conceals a real cost by moving it off the agency’s ledger.

teaching.title: Give the recommendation a fair hearing
teaching.text:
An ethical leader makes the reason for favoring an option available for challenge. A procedural approach establishes who verifies restrictions, approves spending and reviews a contract. A participative approach brings the affected people into the question of what a useful session would provide. Each addresses a different problem. A well-attended meeting cannot authorize spending, and fiscal approval gives little evidence about what a participant will experience.

Draft a recommendation in four sentences. State the public purpose, the two competing uses, the evidence supporting the preferred option, and the uncertainty the decision maker must accept. Include an estimate of staff time. If a supervisor chooses the evening pilot, someone needs to release a worker from another assignment to run it. Once the sessions take place, compare attendance and participant experience with the forecast. Ask who encountered a barrier and what the team can change next cycle. If the balance was spent on time but the intended residents remained unable to participate, the fiscal record can be correct while the service design still needs work.

scenario: A report shows a balance that appears large enough for another community session. Several sessions have occurred but their invoices have not yet been paid.
decision: What check would justify a new commitment?

choices.label: Reconcile approved commitments, services already delivered and payments before reserving another date.
choices.feedback: This separates cash timing from available capacity. Ask the program which costs may still change.

choices.label: Sketch two session options with the program while finance verifies the balance, and mark both as provisional.
choices.feedback: Options help people judge which investment would improve access. Tell partners what is still a possibility so they do not incur costs in reliance on it.

perspective: A partner says the more expensive evening option would reach people who have never been able to attend a daytime session. The cheaper option has space available now.
reconsider: How would you compare reach, evidence of demand and cost once the real balance is known?
reflection: Which apparent saving might only be an unpaid obligation?
transfer: Create a brief recommendation that shows commitments, expected costs and the access evidence needed before an approval.
followup: Reconcile money committed, services delivered and invoices paid before comparing who an added session would reach.
