title: Leading change across an organization
objective: Decide whether to expand a shared process when exceptions have no owner
learn: How to trace who accepts exceptions, who does the extra work and what would trigger a change in the plan

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: Imagine that several units agree to accept referrals through one shared route. At the design meeting, the proposal looks simpler for everyone. At a local partner’s office, a worker is wondering who will answer when someone cannot use that route. At the receiving unit, staff are asking who will own an urgent referral when information is incomplete. Both questions belong in the design of the change. Finding them after launch leaves the people with the fewest choices to work around the problem.

teaching.title: Give the people doing the work decisions to make
teaching.text:
Assemble a group that can follow a referral across the whole service. Include someone who sends it, someone who receives it and people who can describe the process of seeking help. Give members a clear charge. For example, leadership may have set the goal of one point of entry while leaving contact methods and handoff procedures open. Spell out which decisions the group owns, which it can recommend and who can resolve a conflict. Arrange ways for people to contribute around work schedules or outside a large meeting.

Ask each person to trace the same difficult case. Compare where responsibility changes hands. If a partner sees no way to confirm that a referral arrived, make that a design question. Explain why the change is being made, the next decision and the person who can answer operational questions. Publish the answer wherever staff will need it during a shift.

teaching.title: Watch what survives first contact with practice
teaching.text:
Pilot the change on a scale where the team can notice and repair a failure. Check how many referrals reach a named worker and how often a person seeking help has to start again. Debrief with both units. If staff quietly return to a previous process, find out what it allowed them to accomplish. An informal phone call may have prevented someone from being stranded between offices. Retain that function in the new arrangement.

Thank the colleagues who made the earlier system work and the person who points out a defect in the new one. Show what the group changed in response. Staff learn whether leaders welcome difficult news by watching what happens to the first person who brings it.

An organization can invite criticism on a pilot and still discourage it in practice. Ask pilot staff who have seen a flaw to choose a workable way to raise it, give someone the authority to pause or adjust a failing step and explain afterward which observation led to a change. That sequence gives people evidence that leaders will protect room for learning during the rollout.

teaching.title: Trace what a change asks each unit to give up
teaching.text:
Return to the shared referral route. A program manager announces that every unit will use it beginning next month. A receiving supervisor says their team is ready because every worker has access to the system. A county partner says it cannot send urgent information through the new route. An intake worker adds that a telephone handoff has been the only reliable way to confirm that someone in crisis was connected. These are different accounts of readiness. Choosing the most senior person’s account could turn a project milestone into a service failure.

In Coordinating policy changes across units, follow the lesson on tracing a revision through connected work. Use one ordinary referral and one urgent referral as separate examples. Give each unit a chance to explain what it receives, what it can do with that input and how the next person knows it has accepted responsibility. Have the partner make the same journey from outside the agency. Give each unresolved handoff an owner with authority to settle it or a route to someone who can.

teaching.title: Give staff a way to change the rollout
teaching.text:
Transformational leadership can keep people focused on the experience the new arrangement should deliver. Shared leadership puts parts of the design with people who have the needed knowledge. A sponsor might give the receiving unit responsibility for proposing an acknowledgment method and the partner group a real choice about how to receive it. The sponsor should say which common service expectations still apply and how two units can resolve competing requests. A committee with no decisions of its own offers little protection against a flawed design.

At the midpoint, ask what evidence would justify continuing, revising or briefly holding the rollout. For example, sample whether a sender can determine who has the referral without a second call. Check the urgent cases separately because a good overall rate can hide a serious problem in a small group. Give staff time and permission to surface failed transfers while there is still time to repair them. Report back to the pilot group with the change made in response, the decision maker and what happens to the old route. That closes an operational gap that enthusiasm at a launch meeting could never resolve.

scenario: Three units can use one referral route for routine cases. A trial exposes an urgent incomplete referral that the receiving team can record but cannot accept.
decision: Do you expand the route now or resolve the exception before adding units?

choices.label: Keep the pilot bounded and name someone with authority to accept or redirect urgent exceptions.
choices.feedback: You protect the next resident while gathering evidence. Set a deadline so the pilot does not become permanent without a decision.

choices.label: Expand only the routine route and retain an explicit, staffed exception route during the next trial.
choices.feedback: More staff can learn the common process. Verify that workers can distinguish the routes and partners know whom to contact when the distinction is unclear.

perspective: Frontline staff say the urgent flag is seen only after the receiving unit has accepted the referral.
reconsider: What change would let staff act before the person falls between the two systems?
reflection: Which unit appears efficient because another unit absorbs the workaround?
transfer: Test the proposed route on an incomplete urgent case after hours. Record who accepts the next action and when an expansion decision can be revisited.
followup: Trace who can accept the exception, who would do extra work and what would trigger a change in the rollout.
track: Track 3: Leading people through change; Track 4: Leading across DHS

title: Turning a strategic priority into a plan
objective: Choose which improvement to test first and what can wait
learn: How to define success with the people who use the service, name the decision owner and set the evidence for further investment

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: Suppose a division wants Minnesotans to get a useful answer the first time they ask for help. One leader proposes a new website. Another proposes adding people to the phones. Before committing to either, the team needs to know what a useful answer means to the people calling, who can change the experience, and which competing work it is prepared to defer. Strategic planning gives staff and partners a way to make those choices together.

teaching.title: Establish the purpose and examine the current experience
teaching.text:
The sponsor can begin by naming the decision the plan will guide, the people who can commit resources and the constraints the group will face. Invite staff who receive questions and partners who hear what happens afterward. Ask each person to describe a recent contact that worked well and one that required a second attempt. Compare those accounts with available service data. A short call might mean the question was answered quickly. It might also mean the caller was referred elsewhere and still needs help.

Identify what you know well enough to act on, what remains uncertain and whose experience is missing. Give one person responsibility for filling a consequential evidence gap. Time spent gathering more information should reflect how much it could change the decision.

teaching.title: Choose a direction and give the first steps owners
teaching.text:
Return to the program’s mission to check that the ambition fits its purpose. Picture the difference people could experience in three to five years. Choose a small number of strategies the team can pursue over the next year or two, then assign actions for the next three to six months. For example, if workers in two units give conflicting answers, reconcile those answers and test a common response before investing in a new contact channel.

Write the first assignment so the person taking it can tell when it is done. Name who can approve a corrected answer, when front-line staff will try it and how the team will learn whether it helped. At the next planning meeting, review what happened to the people seeking help. If the evidence changes the team’s view of the problem, make the adjustment visible to the people who helped set the direction.

Use appreciative inquiry when part of the service already works well. Invite a worker and a partner to reconstruct a successful contact and identify which conditions made it possible. Decide which of those conditions the strategy could reproduce elsewhere and what additional evidence would be needed before doing so.

teaching.title: Negotiate what would count as improvement
teaching.text:
In a planning session, three units endorse the goal of answering more questions on first contact. They mean different things. One counts a call routed to the right unit as answered. Another counts it only when a worker explains the next step. A resident who has received the same referral twice may judge success by whether the receiving office actually responds. A plan that leaves all three definitions in place could report improvement while staff and residents experience continuing difficulty.

Use Setting equity measures and targets to work through the lesson on the recorded event. Ask each unit to show which event its available information captures and what the record leaves unknown. Agree on a measure people can interpret today and a method for learning about the missing part. A short, optional follow-up with a small group of callers might reveal whether the answer was usable. A finding from that small group can inform a decision without supporting a claim about every caller. Identify who could be systematically missed, including people who never get through the queue.

teaching.title: Choose a first investment under constraint
teaching.text:
The team has capacity for one pilot. Digital staff propose revised search terms to help residents find an answer on the website. Program staff propose a pilot that connects callers directly to a receiving unit. Use an adaptive leadership approach when the teams hold different beliefs about what successful access looks like. Give each a chance to show where its proposal would make the greatest difference and which residents would still encounter difficulty. Then have the named decision maker choose a pilot and state the reason. A choice to try one option now should leave the other team clear about what future evidence would reopen the decision.

Translate the pilot into a short agreement. Identify the service group, the baseline observation, the person responsible for implementation, the source of follow-up information and the date of the first adjustment. If the team can document faster routing but cannot yet establish whether residents received an answer, report both facts. Strategic leadership includes resisting pressure to declare success simply because the activities in the plan have been completed.

scenario: Leaders want a useful answer at the first contact. A new script, protected callback time and an improved transfer process all compete for one team's attention.
decision: Which improvement will you test first and what will wait?

choices.label: Test a transfer in which the receiving team confirms ownership before the first team closes the request.
choices.feedback: This directly addresses lost handoffs. Check whether the receiving team can absorb confirmation work and whether residents know what happens next.

choices.label: Test a script that distinguishes questions staff can answer today from ones requiring follow-up.
choices.feedback: Clear language can prevent false expectations. The script cannot supply an owner for an unanswered question by itself.

perspective: Residents in the trial say they do not always need a final answer today. Knowing who is responsible and when they will hear back matters more.
reconsider: How would their definition of useful change the trial, measure and scope?
reflection: Who should be able to challenge the proposed success measure?
transfer: Draft a first-month test naming an owner, an activity to defer and a point at which you would reconsider the investment.
followup: Define a useful answer with people who use the service. Name the decision owner and the evidence that would justify further investment.
track: Track 3: Leading people through change; Track 4: Sustaining change

title: Setting a vision people can use
objective: Use a vision to choose between two good investments
learn: How to explain a choice through the vision and name the evidence that could change it

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: Two teams may agree on their purpose and still disagree about what to fund next. A mission explains why the work exists. A vision describes a future the organization hopes to bring about. Its value shows up when two worthwhile choices compete for the same time or money. Ask whether a colleague could use the proposed vision to choose between them and explain that choice to a person affected by it.

teaching.title: Start with a scene from the future
teaching.text:
Invite colleagues and people with experience of the service to picture an ordinary day three to five years from now. What would someone trying to reach the right worker be able to do? What would a new employee see an experienced colleague doing differently? Collect individual answers before opening the discussion so the first person to speak has less influence over what others consider possible. Give people another way to contribute if they prefer to write or need more time.

Suppose one person imagines leaving a call knowing who owns the next step. Another pictures being able to communicate in the way that works for them. A third wants staff to see whether help actually arrived. List the specific changes embedded in those answers. A small drafting group can bring back language that captures the shared ambition. Let participants say what the draft gets right, what it drops and whether anyone would read it as a promise the organization cannot keep.

teaching.title: Try the words against a real choice
teaching.text:
A candidate vision for this exercise might be, “People who contact us know who will follow up, when to expect an answer and how to reach us if the plan changes.” Give the group two proposals: redesign the home page or give receiving teams a reliable way to confirm a handoff. Ask which would move practice closer to the envisioned experience and what evidence would change their answer. Either could be right under different conditions.

Use the agreed wording when setting priorities and when explaining a decision to staff. Revisit it as community needs and program responsibilities change. If nobody can point to a decision it has influenced, bring a specific upcoming choice back to the group and see where the language needs work.

teaching.title: Hear what people mean by the same promise
teaching.text:
Suppose a division chooses “responsive service” as its ambition. To a phone worker that means answering quickly. To a disability advocate it means a caller can use the channel they choose. To a partner with a complex question it may mean one person remains responsible until a usable answer arrives. A leader can gather unanimous support for those two words and still have no agreement about what a Tuesday afternoon should look like. Ask people to supply the experience behind the word they support.

Team values that guide real decisions offers a way to examine competing meanings of a shared word. Apply it to a choice between a rapid callback promise and a longer appointment with a person who can resolve several questions. For each option, ask who gains time, who must do more work and which part of the agency promise the option keeps. Where a person needs an accessible way to participate, identify the responsible process and resources. A general vote about customer preferences would leave that particular obligation unresolved.

teaching.title: Give people a way to challenge the picture
teaching.text:
A charismatic presentation may draw attention to a goal. The test comes after the presentation, when a supervisor must decide which kind of contact staff are rewarded for completing. If the supervisor recognizes only the shortest calls, workers learn a narrower meaning of responsiveness than the director described. Invite a staff member to show one instance where the performance measure and the vision point in different directions. The director should name who can change that measure and invite a practical alternative.

Transformational leadership can give people a shared sense of direction across units. A transformative or equity-centered approach adds a question about the rule itself. Who selected speed as the only visible sign of a good service, who has been carrying the cost, and who can change the measure? Keep one example of the decision the team revised and let the people affected describe the result. That gives a new employee something concrete to learn from, and a person outside the agency a reasonable way to judge whether the vision has influenced the service.

scenario: A division envisions a service where residents can tell what will happen next. One team proposes a redesigned homepage. Another proposes requiring the receiving team to confirm a handoff.
decision: What evidence would make either investment a stronger first choice?

choices.label: Compare where residents first lose the next step and test a confirmation at that point.
choices.feedback: If uncertainty begins after submission, the trial reaches the right problem. Consider people who never reach submission.

choices.label: Test the existing homepage with someone trying to find the service for the first time.
choices.feedback: A navigation problem may justify redesign. Include the later handoff before declaring the whole journey usable.

perspective: One person found the right program immediately but waited without confirmation. Another used an outdated contact page and never reached the program.
reconsider: How would you decide which improvement goes first and what evidence would reopen that decision?
reflection: Whose version of a successful service appears in your vision?
transfer: Write a one-sentence vision and use it to defend a choice between the two investments, including a reason to change course.
followup: Use the proposed vision to explain the choice, and identify evidence that could make the other investment more valuable.

title: Making a decision when the cause is uncertain
objective: Help the person waiting today while you investigate the cause
learn: How to trace where guidance first diverged, and why a safe interim answer and a verified cause can come at different times

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A supervisor asks for refresher training because several people received conflicting instructions. Training could help. It could also leave a careful employee following one of two contradictory instructions with greater confidence. The leader’s first responsibility is to define the difficulty precisely enough that the team can investigate it and decide how quickly somebody needs an answer.

teaching.title: Follow the work to the point where it diverges
teaching.text:
Choose a recent example that can be discussed without identifying the person who sought help. Ask a worker from each team to demonstrate how they arrive at an answer. Look at the information available to them at that moment. Suppose both workers followed written guidance and the two documents give different directions. The team has found a cause that a reminder about diligence would leave untouched. If both documents agree, investigate other explanations, such as unclear exceptions or different information available on different shifts.

Agree on the consequence that matters. In this example, the person had to telephone twice and still did not know what to do next. Ask what already works in comparable cases. A colleague on another shift may know who resolves exceptions promptly. Sometimes making that route visible addresses the difficulty without creating a new project.

teaching.title: Make a proportionate decision and check the result
teaching.text:
Identify who can issue an authoritative clarification. While that person resolves the discrepancy, a supervisor might arrange a common contact for cases in doubt and tell staff how to reach them. Give this interim decision an owner and an end date. Explain what is still uncertain so staff can answer questions accurately. If delay itself carries a cost, include that cost when weighing an interim arrangement against waiting for a permanent answer.

Once guidance is corrected, ask two people who were outside the working group to use it on the same situation. Compare the answers and see whether a caller would know the next step. Look again after a few weeks to see whether the conflict has returned. Tell the staff who first raised the concern what the organization changed and whether it helped.

teaching.title: Find out who carries the cost of an interim answer
teaching.text:
Once two units discover their instructions conflict, agreeing that someone should fix the guidance is easy. The harder decision is what a person seeking help will experience until the correction is ready. One team may want to review all current cases immediately. The other has work due that day and can review only cases in which an unresolved question will cause a delay. A leader who tells both teams to make it their highest priority has assigned the same hours twice.

Open Resolving cross-unit priority conflicts and use the lesson on consequences and capacity. Set out what each team is trying to protect. Estimate how much time the review takes, which employees can do it and which work they would set aside. Compare two genuine alternatives. One might provide a named contact today for people facing an immediate consequence and schedule a broader review tomorrow. The other might assign a separate unit to help review, provided that unit has the knowledge and authority. A supervisor who favors either proposal should explain who will wait, for how long and what to do if circumstances change.

teaching.title: Distinguish a decision from a diagnosis
teaching.text:
A directive response can be appropriate for the immediate instruction that everyone needs before a shift starts. It does little to explain why the conflict arose or why it escaped review. Delegate investigation to a person who can see how both instructions were revised and circulated. Equip them to talk with front-line staff who may have discovered the ambiguity earlier. Ask where they tried to send the question and what happened to it. An overlooked inbox, a copy saved on a shared drive and two owners who both expected the other to update the guidance call for different corrections.

Set a date for the two teams to test what changed. Give each the same unfamiliar example, ask them to show the source they used, and check what the person seeking help would hear. If both teams now give the same incorrect answer, consistency has improved while accuracy has not. Have the responsible program specialist judge the answer and a worker from outside the design group judge whether it can be put into practice. Those two checks give the leader a better basis for closing the issue.

scenario: Two workers have given a resident different instructions. A manager suggests a refresher course. The person still needs to know what to do today.
decision: What can you do for the person while investigating the cause?

choices.label: Verify the current instruction with its owner and arrange one accountable follow-up to the resident.
choices.feedback: This limits the immediate burden. Trace how each worker reached a different answer before designing training.

choices.label: Compare both instructions step by step, while another authorized colleague handles the urgent individual question.
choices.feedback: You can identify the first point of divergence. Give the resident a usable time or channel for an update while this happens.

perspective: Both workers used the same reference. Their screens exposed different versions because the team links were different.
reconsider: Which part of the response still calls for instruction, and which part requires a system owner?
reflection: What cost did the resident bear while staff looked for a cause?
transfer: Trace a second fictional inquiry after correcting the links. Identify what would still justify training.
followup: Trace the first point where the guidance diverged. A safe interim answer and a verified cause may arrive at different times.

title: Working with partners and the public
objective: Make an invitation worth a partner's time
learn: How to state the decision, its limits, who can change it and when partners will hear how their input was used

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A community organization receives an invitation to “give feedback on service access.” Its staff have spent months telling agencies that many of their clients cannot answer a daytime call. Before accepting another invitation, they want to know which decision is open and whether anyone at the meeting can change it. A leader can answer those questions in the invitation itself. Doing so lets potential participants judge whether contributing is worth their time and what experience would be most useful.

teaching.title: Invite people into a decision they can influence
teaching.text:
Suppose the decision concerns how a team offers callbacks. Explain what the team can change, what is fixed for now and when it will choose. Ask a question a person can answer from experience: “When we offered to call back, what made it possible or difficult for you to take that call?” Say how someone can respond, whom to contact for access needs and when contributors will hear back. An invitation that goes only to established partners can miss people who stopped trying to reach the program. Ask who else should have a way in.

Offer workable options such as a short phone conversation, a written response or a discussion through a trusted partner. Ask the partner what support participation would take. Avoid treating a partner’s perspective as a substitute for everyone it serves. Those who handle requests every day and those who have repeatedly missed a callback each know something the other may never see.

teaching.title: Show what happened to the input
teaching.text:
When reviewing responses, keep differences visible. A scheduled call may work for someone who can reserve a lunch break. A person with an unpredictable shift may value an agreed alternative if the first call is missed. Counting which option received more mentions will not tell you how well either serves people in those circumstances.

Report the decision in language a contributor can recognize. Describe what you heard, what you will try, what you could not adopt and why. Give the change a review date and a person who can receive further concerns. When the pilot ends, ask whether people actually reached a worker. The people who gave the agency their time deserve to know what difference it made.

teaching.title: Let a person change the design
teaching.text:
A staff team draws two possible callback arrangements on paper. One offers a fixed appointment. The other offers an evening window. A participant who uses disability services says that neither solves the difficulty. The problem is that the phone displays an unfamiliar number, and they cannot tell a service call from an unwanted one. Their sister offers to take all the calls instead. The team now has three perspectives: the person’s experience, a family member’s useful offer and the agency’s concern about missed contacts. Each deserves attention. Only the person can tell the team which role they want their sister to have.

Work through Designing with people with disabilities and families. Use two simple versions of the proposed arrangement so participants can point to what they would keep, remove or replace. Ask the person how they want to be involved, whom they would like alongside them and what choice they would make if the team could change one more thing. Discuss a recognizable callback arrangement or a mutually agreed cue with the appropriate service owner. Leave room for the person to reject both initial proposals. Offering options matters only if the available choices can respond to what the person has said.

teaching.title: Make the limits of shared authority visible
teaching.text:
Participative leadership works here when participants can influence the actual design. A leader can also delegate the choice of a pilot question to the people who will try it, with a clear account of constraints. Be careful with the phrase “the community agreed.” One person may prefer advance notice, another may need flexibility, and others may have had no opportunity to respond. Record which feedback led to which revision, where people differed and which decision remains with an authorized manager.

At the next meeting, bring the revised design and ask participants to use it in a realistic situation. Someone who can predict which call to answer has learned something about the new arrangement. The agency still needs experience from ordinary operation to decide whether it improves contact rates or reduces repeated work. Return a short account to participants in the formats they can use. That return lets them correct a mistaken interpretation before it becomes part of an agency decision.

scenario: A partner has repeatedly explained why daytime calls are difficult. The agency invites them to another discussion. The location is fixed, but the callback windows and follow-up method can still change.
decision: What would make the invitation worth the partner's time?

choices.label: Identify exactly which scheduling choices remain open, who can decide them, and when the partner will hear back.
choices.feedback: The partner can judge whether participation is worthwhile. Budget for the actual work of gathering input where authority allows.

choices.label: Share what happened to earlier feedback and ask how the partner wants to contribute to the current choice.
choices.feedback: This acknowledges the existing relationship. Explain the new limits before inviting the partner to gather more views.

perspective: The partner says they can share two experiences directly. Collecting a broader response would require time their organization has not agreed to provide.
reconsider: How will you use the information honestly and avoid treating two accounts as the community's decision?
reflection: What does a contributor need to know when the agency cannot adopt their suggestion?
transfer: Draft a report-back message giving a decision, its basis, what remains open and a realistic date for the next communication.
followup: State the decision, its limits, who can change it and when partners will hear how their input was used.

title: Speaking to reporters on behalf of an agency
objective: Respond to a reporter's deadline accurately and route what you cannot answer
learn: How to verify facts, separate one person's experience from program-wide evidence, and tell residents what they can do meanwhile

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A local reporter calls late in the morning about residents who say they could not reach a program the day before. The reporter goes on air at noon. A staff member may know that their own phone was working, but that observation says little about the experience across the service. A useful first response is to capture the question, the affected time and place, the deadline and a way to get back in touch. Route the request to the designated spokesperson or communications team.

teaching.title: Prepare an answer that a resident can act on
teaching.text:
If you have been assigned to speak, work with the people who can verify the facts. Find out which service was affected, what people should do now and which questions remain open. Agree on a time to provide an update. Acknowledge the request promptly, including when verification will take longer than the reporter’s deadline. A callback promise works only if someone has taken responsibility for making it.

For practice, imagine a voicemail queue failed on Tuesday morning. A program lead can verify the hours affected and that the queue is working again. They cannot yet say how many messages were lost. Construct a short response with those boundaries in place. Lead with the hours affected, give residents a verified way to reach the program and explain when you expect to know more about the messages. Avoid naming a cause while it is still under investigation.

teaching.title: Rehearse the difficult follow-up
teaching.text:
Ask a colleague to play the reporter and press you on something you cannot confirm. Pause, answer the part you know and be direct about what you still need to check. If asked about an individual’s experience, stick to information you are authorized to share and explain how someone can seek help privately. An accurate response should still make sense if one sentence from it is broadcast alone.

Before the interview, say the essential information aloud at a conversational pace. Afterward, check that any promised information reached the reporter and that the service route you described remains usable. Respect for the reporter’s work and for residents’ time is visible in the accuracy of that follow-through.

teaching.title: Prepare for a question about unequal effects
teaching.text:
Imagine that a reporter follows up on the missed messages. A partner says callers who needed an interpreter waited longer, and asks whether the department treated people differently. A spokesperson needs to take the concern seriously and describe the evidence accurately. One caller’s account can identify a failure the agency should examine. It does not establish how widespread the failure was. An overall average wait time cannot settle whether people experienced a consistent difference across languages.

In Communicating disparity findings with care, look at how to describe the measure and the limits of the comparison. Prepare a short working note with the date range, which contacts are included, what a wait measures and what happened to unreturned calls in the count. Ask a program colleague who knows the actual service how interpreter requests are recorded. If an unreturned message has no language information, the absence of a label may hide the people most affected. Make that limitation part of the analysis before the agency offers a public conclusion.

teaching.title: Use authority to make accuracy possible
teaching.text:
An ethical approach makes clear which facts a spokesperson can verify now and what the agency is doing about the concern. A procedural approach ensures that the person authorized to share the information checks it, including the risk of identifying an individual through a very small group. An inclusive approach helps the team learn from people whose experience is missing from an internal dashboard. The public interview itself should leave people able to distinguish those three activities.

Rehearse a follow-up with a colleague. The reporter asks whether the figures disprove the partner’s account. Start with the finding you can support, explain in everyday terms which callers the figure leaves out, and give a realistic point of contact for an update. If people need assistance now, provide a verified route they can use. Have a second reader underline every statement that could be mistaken for a conclusion about why the problem occurred. Revise those sentences before the deadline. After the update, contact the relevant program owner about the practical question the reporting uncovered. A carefully worded answer earns its value when the agency also learns enough to improve what residents encounter.

scenario: A reporter going on air at noon asks about yesterday's service interruption. A worker can describe their own desk but has no verified figure for the whole program.
decision: Which response can you prepare within your role?

choices.label: Record the question and deadline, refer the inquiry to the authorized communications contact, and verify the route residents can use now.
choices.feedback: This supports a useful and accurate response. Confirm that the alternative route actually works before passing it on.

choices.label: Collect verified details from the service owner and prepare a short set of facts and open questions for the authorized spokesperson.
choices.feedback: A briefing can help the spokesperson explain uncertainty. Communicate the deadline immediately so gathering detail does not consume the whole response window.

perspective: The reporter asks whether the interruption affected people using interpreters more often. Existing outage logs record time offline but do not identify those experiences.
reconsider: What can be verified now, whose perspective should be sought, and when could the question be revisited?
reflection: How might a confident comment from one person be heard as an agency-wide conclusion?
transfer: Draft a factual update for the appropriate reviewer with an actionable next step for residents and one explicitly unresolved question.
followup: Record the deadline and distinguish one worker’s experience from evidence about people trying to reach the whole program.

title: Workload prioritization
theme: Teams and the work they carry
objective: Decide what needs action first when several urgent demands collide
learn: How to weigh the cost of delay for each person affected, fix the most harmful problem first, and say which commitment moves

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A phone number on a public referral page is wrong. A partner needs a decision about an event. A director has asked for presentation slides by Friday. All three requests have arrived before lunch. The order in which messages arrived tells you little about how long people can afford to wait. Prioritizing work requires a judgment about consequences. Someone needs to be able to explain that judgment to the people whose work will move.

teaching.title: Compare the consequences of waiting
teaching.text:
Start with your role and the outcomes your team has agreed to deliver. Include routine service, commitments to partners, and time set aside to develop a skill. An inventory helps you see an important piece of work that nobody is emailing about. For each item, identify who needs the result, the earliest step someone else is waiting for, and the deadline you can confirm. Ask the requester where a date came from. A presentation due Friday may be needed in accessible form on Wednesday.

Consider impact and effort together. Correcting the phone number could take ten minutes and spare callers repeated failed attempts. Replacing an entire directory could benefit many more people and require several weeks. Give the correction immediate attention and reserve time for the larger repair. A small formatting preference can wait for a scheduled update. A laborious redesign that serves no identified need deserves a conversation before anyone starts it. A fixed service obligation still needs time even when it scores poorly on a convenience measure.

teaching.title: Make the choice visible
teaching.text:
Check your order with the people who depend on it. You may learn that the partner only needs a room capacity today and can wait for the complete agenda. Offer that smaller decision, identify who will confirm it, and tell the director when the slides will be ready. When tradeoffs are close, agree on criteria such as service impact, timing, and the number of teams waiting. Give the most important criterion greater weight and discuss any ranking that surprises the group.

Put the first action on your calendar and contact the person authorized to correct the number. Reserve the next block of time for the directory. At your next check-in, ask which consequence you anticipated correctly and what new information changed the order. A useful priority decision gives colleagues enough notice to change their own plans.

teaching.title: When a quick repair competes with a lasting improvement
teaching.text:
Correcting the referral number solves today's error. A colleague discovers that three units maintain their own copies of the same contact list. Correcting every copy will take an afternoon. Establishing a reliable owner and a way to tell partners about changes will take a month. Give those two pieces of work separate places in the plan. Otherwise the quick correction may be reported as a permanent solution, or the search for a permanent solution may leave a wrong number on the page for another week.

An impact and effort grid helps separate readily achievable changes, substantial investments, convenient low-value tasks and work that consumes considerable effort for little return. Decide whose effort counts. One hour saved at the central office may cost twenty partner sites an hour each. Before rating the benefit, ask who uses the number, what happens after a failed call and whether there is another usable way to reach the service. Staff do not need to know a caller's identity to find out whether the published route works.

For a closer choice, agree on criteria and weights before rating the proposals. If preventing interruption to a public service counts twice as much as convenience for staff, write that down. Try the ranking again with a smaller weight. If the first and second choices switch places, explain the disputed judgment to the person with authority to decide. A weighted matrix is especially valuable when it reveals why two reasonable people disagree.

teaching.title: Choose when to direct and when to invite judgment
teaching.text:
Compare Autocratic or directive leadership with Democratic or participative leadership in the leadership styles collection. Have two colleagues rehearse the opening minute after the error is discovered. The first assigns a person to correct the number immediately and names who will verify it. The second asks partner offices how numbers are kept current and which notification method they already use. The first response suits an immediate correction. The second gives people who maintain the network a say in how it will work. Using either approach throughout would leave part of the problem unsolved.

Reserve time for the longer repair alongside development commitments and recurring work. Agree on a review date with the person whose presentation was delayed. The first action can be as short as opening each public listing and recording where the number appears. Once repairs are in place, ask a colleague outside the team to follow the route. Look at what the caller can now do and whether the team can explain who will catch the next change.

scenario: A published referral number is wrong. A partner is waiting to book space. A set of slides is due Friday. Three owners describe their item as urgent.
decision: What will you address first, and who needs notice of the trade-off?

choices.label: Assign the referral repair now and ask someone to find the partner's last decision time.
choices.feedback: This can reduce immediate harm without losing the chance to book. Name who will reconnect people who already used the wrong number.

choices.label: Arrange a temporary working contact while the page owner verifies the correction, then settle the booking deadline.
choices.feedback: This can serve people during the repair. Tell the slides owner what work has moved and when the new deadline is feasible.

perspective: A service worker says correcting the website will miss people who received paper copies with the incorrect number.
reconsider: How would you divide the quick repair from the lasting follow-up?
reflection: Who pays for a delay that never appears on your task list?
transfer: Order the next three actions with owners and times. Include one commitment you would explicitly renegotiate.
followup: Weigh the cost of delay for each person. Assign the immediate repair and communicate which other commitment moves.

title: Why plan your workload?
theme: Teams and the work they carry
objective: Bring commitments back within available hours
learn: How to count hidden work such as preparation, access arrangements, coaching and follow-up, and avoid overloading the next period

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A calendar can show a full week of appointments while hiding the work each appointment creates. A one-hour community conversation may require two hours to prepare, another to arrange access, and several more to verify and report what people said. A workload plan puts that labor in view early enough for a supervisor and employee to make different commitments.

teaching.title: Draw a picture of the next few weeks
teaching.text:
Choose a period long enough to see a collision coming. Start with three two-week columns on paper or in a spreadsheet. Give each major responsibility a row. Include everyday service, project work, preparation, follow-up, staff development, and planned time away. Keep the categories broad enough that maintaining the plan takes only a few minutes. If hours are difficult to estimate, shade a small, medium, or large share of each period. Use a label as well as shading so another reader can interpret the estimate.

Suppose an analyst has 64 hours available in the next period after planned leave. Routine requests typically take 32 hours. Preparing a partner workshop takes 18. The analyst expects to spend 16 hours on a report and four coaching a new colleague. The plan calls for 70 hours. A six-hour gap can look manageable until an unexpected service question consumes the only unscheduled afternoon. Ask which estimate is most uncertain and what the people doing the work have learned from a similar period.

teaching.title: Use the plan to change a commitment
teaching.text:
The supervisor can ask the workshop owner whether someone else can prepare the materials, or whether the report reader needs the whole report at once. If the analyst can deliver validated figures this week and commentary next week, check that the later period has room and notify the reader. Protecting coaching time also has a work consequence. The new colleague may take on part of the next report once they have practiced with support.

Use the next check-in to compare estimated and actual effort. If routine requests took 40 hours, revise that row and discuss the continuing effect. A useful plan allows both people to see who authorized a change, when relief will arrive, and whether moving work has simply created a new peak two weeks later.

teaching.title: Separate work time from waiting time
teaching.text:
A meeting with community advisers may need a month of lead time even if its organizer spends only three days working on it. Someone must confirm a date, arrange communication supports, send material early enough for advisers to review it, and allow contributors to correct the record. These activities do different things to the plan. Reserving a room consumes little staff time but may control the date of everything else. Reviewing responses takes longer and may be possible while the team waits for confirmations.

On a copy of the plan, mark the earliest date each task can start, the person or response it depends on and the latest useful completion date. Ask people who usually do the work to review the estimates. Include regular supervision, required learning and recurring office coverage. If a bilingual colleague has been helping staff navigate questions about access arrangements, find out what that support takes. Make responsibility explicit and arrange appropriate language services where needed. Unassigned work is easily mistaken for spare capacity.

Use Make participation more accessible to examine the event before promising an attendance date. Its questions about preparing multiple ways to contribute can uncover tasks the plan missed. For an evening gathering, for instance, someone needs to receive daytime written comments, bring them into the discussion and get back to the contributors. Put that time and an owner in the plan. Someone checking the calendar should be able to see which part could move and what people would lose if it did.

teaching.title: Plan for a disruption before it happens
teaching.text:
Rehearse two versions of the week. In one, both staff responsible for arranging the session are available. In the other, one covers an unplanned vacancy. What can a backup take over with the information already available? Which choice needs a manager? Shared or distributed leadership can give a second employee authority to make routine arrangements. That authority needs to exist before a rushed handoff. A colleague who knows the history but cannot confirm a booking can only report what is about to go wrong.

At the next check-in, compare the forecast with the work actually done by category. A single unexpected absence is poor grounds for a permanent redesign. Repeated weeks in which access preparation or community follow-up has to happen after hours point to a problem in the allocation itself. Change the estimate, assign coverage or reduce the volume promised. Tell the people expecting the work which decision was made and when they can rely on the revised plan.

scenario: An analyst has 64 available hours and 70 hours of commitments this period. The estimate excludes some access arrangements and coaching time. Managers have agreed that each deliverable matters.
decision: Which scope or timing decision would make the plan feasible?

choices.label: Narrow one deliverable with its owner, recover the detailed estimate and review the trade-off with the receiving team.
choices.feedback: Scope changes can free real capacity. Check that unfinished work has not simply moved to a team with even less room.

choices.label: Move one due date after checking the next period's existing commitments and waiting time.
choices.feedback: The current week can fit. A visible later date is useful only if the next period really has capacity for the deferred work.

perspective: The proposed six hours of relief include two hours spent waiting for a response while other work can proceed. A colleague also does two hours of unrecorded coordination.
reconsider: How much working time did the change actually free?
reflection: What part of your original estimate disappeared because nobody had named an owner?
transfer: Build the next period with available work hours, waiting time and one contingency shown separately. Test it against an unplanned absence.
followup: Account for preparation, access arrangements, coaching and follow-up. Check that the change does not overload the next period.

title: Asking leadership for a workable plan
theme: Teams and the work they carry
objective: Bring a clear trade-off to the person who sets priorities
learn: How to present a workable choice, its effect on service and a time for an answer, and who else needs to hear it

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: “When another urgent request comes in, which commitment should I move?” is a question an employee can reasonably put to a supervisor. It asks the person who can set priorities to make a decision. This matters when different managers have each approved work without seeing their combined effect on the people carrying it out.

teaching.title: Show the pattern and its cost
teaching.text:
Look back over a representative stretch of work. Record what was assigned, what changed, where time went, and who experienced a delay. Include repetitive work, hours beyond the usual schedule, and previous attempts to simplify the process. One unusually busy day may call for short-term help. The same clash every reporting cycle calls for a decision about ownership, staffing, or scope. Use examples that describe the work without disclosing private information about people served.

Imagine a specialist who covers a public inbox and prepares a recurring partner briefing. On three successive briefing days, two teams independently requested the same figures in different formats. The specialist prepared both and left inbox coverage to a colleague who had not been told to expect it. Each manager saw a report arrive on time. Neither could see the colleague’s interrupted work or the time spent reconciling two versions.

teaching.title: Ask for a decision someone can carry out
teaching.text:
Bring a recommendation and a real alternative. “I can prepare one set of figures for both teams if they agree on the definitions by Tuesday. If both versions are essential, I need someone assigned to the inbox on briefing mornings. Which can we arrange?” Ask what constraint you might be missing. One audience may genuinely need a different reporting period. The supervisor can negotiate that distinction while the specialist estimates the additional work.

Write down the decision, the person who will speak with the other managers, and the date you will see whether it helped. If nothing changes, bring the specific unresolved commitment back before its next deadline. Explain what fits within your available hours and what still needs a decision. If an ongoing problem persists, a mentor, another appropriate leader, or Human Resources can help identify how to raise it. The employee can describe the collision. Management has to decide how the organization will absorb it.

teaching.title: Make conflicting assignments visible without putting colleagues on trial
teaching.text:
An employee can bring a real constraint into the room without disclosing personal information about the people served. Prepare a short account of the competing work. For each commitment, identify who authorized it, the latest useful date, what has already been done and the consequence of delay. Include unplanned tasks that arrived during the last comparable period. Repeated requests for help may explain why an assignment that takes four uninterrupted hours has stayed open for a week.

At the meeting, show the supervisor two achievable sequences. For example, an analyst could deliver an estimate before a partner's budget meeting and defer formatting a dashboard, or complete the dashboard first and give the partner a date for validated numbers. A third option might be to send an unverified estimate. Explain what someone could wrongly commit to if they mistook that number for a verified one. The supervisor can now weigh a scheduling cost against an information risk. A worker should not have to settle that tradeoff simply by responding to the loudest request.

If the direction is “both by Friday,” ask what support or change in scope makes that feasible. Perhaps the dashboard can use an existing layout and the estimate needs a second analyst's review. Identify both contributors and make sure they know the assignment has changed. After the conversation, tell each requester what will arrive and when. That also gives a supervisor the chance to correct a misunderstanding before other people build their plans around it.

teaching.title: Practice what happens when the answer does not resolve the issue
teaching.text:
Use Leadership style scenarios with a supervisor or peer. The pathway asks learners to evaluate responses to situations where people hold different amounts of authority. Apply that reasoning to workload. One person plays a manager who controls the deadline. The other plays the only analyst who knows the validation step. Repeat the exchange with the manager taking a coaching approach, drawing out estimates and alternatives, then taking a directive approach to choosing the order once those facts are clear.

Look for two things in the response. Can the employee raise a material concern without being treated as uncooperative? Can both people state who decided and who will inform the other manager? If the manager declines to choose and deadlines remain incompatible, send a brief account of the remaining decision through the ordinary management channel. State the earliest time a choice would prevent harm. Where the pattern persists, a higher-level scheduling discussion or advice from an appropriate workplace resource may help clarify who can resolve it.

scenario: Two managers have already approved work for the same week. One promises a revised service letter to a county on Thursday. The other promises coaching for six new intake workers on Wednesday. An urgent request arrives Tuesday. Each manager can see only their own queue.
decision: What can you bring to the person who can change the commitments?

choices.label: Offer two feasible schedules, show the effect on residents and new workers, and ask for a decision before noon.
choices.feedback: The manager has an actual trade-off to settle. Confirm who will tell the county and who will arrange support for new staff if coaching moves.

choices.label: Ask the managers to agree on the highest priority at their next meeting.
choices.feedback: Joint ownership matters, but the regular meeting is Friday. Name the earliest irreversible step and ask for a decision before it occurs.

perspective: A county partner explains that moving Thursday's letter by one day will miss its weekly print run. The new workers, meanwhile, could join an experienced team for one morning.
reconsider: How does that information change the two schedules you would put forward?
reflection: When have you absorbed conflicting promises in your own working hours?
transfer: Bring one competing deadline to its decision owner with two options, affected people, a decision time and a named person to tell each partner.
followup: Present a feasible choice, its effect on service and a time for an answer. Identify who else needs to hear the decision.

title: Managing a project from assignment to handoff
objective: Bring scope and timing changes to the sponsor without losing quality
learn: How to protect testing with real readers, name the approver and make sure the receiving office uses the right version

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: Suppose a program team has promised to revise an appointment letter for a pilot with two partner offices. One colleague knows the service rules, another writes in plain language, and a third coordinates release. Each understands a different piece of the work. The project manager gives them a shared definition of a finished letter and a way to make decisions when time, cost, and quality pull in different directions.

teaching.title: Define what finished means
teaching.text:
Agree with the sponsor on the people who will use the letter, the problem it should solve, and the scope of the pilot. For example, readers should be able to identify the appointment date, arrange a change, and find help in a format they can use. Identify who can approve the wording and who will authorize distribution. A team can complete a beautiful draft and still miss its deadline if no one has secured a decision from the person who owns the outgoing communication.

Work backward from the first mailing. A printer needs a release file. The release file depends on accessible formatting and a final review. Testing a draft with readers can expose confusing instructions early enough to change them. Ask each contributor what they need from the previous person and when. Estimate the staff time involved, including what other work someone would give up to accelerate a review.

teaching.title: Bring the sponsor an actual choice
teaching.text:
Halfway through the pilot, a partner asks to add a second letter type. The project manager can describe how much design and testing that adds and put alternatives before the sponsor. Keep the agreed mailing date for the first letter and schedule the second, or extend the pilot with both offices’ agreement. Record who chose the option and who needs to hear about it. A short check-in focused on outstanding decisions can be more useful than another meeting where everyone recounts their week.

At handoff, have someone who did not write the letter locate the approved version and explain how a later correction would reach both offices. Give the person maintaining it the decision history, the open questions, and a date for reviewing early feedback. That last exchange turns a temporary project into a piece of work people can sustain.

teaching.title: A late request changes more than the schedule
teaching.text:
Halfway through the letter pilot, a partner asks the project manager to add instructions for appealing a decision. Residents have been asking about that process, and the request deserves attention. It may also change who must review the content, which versions need revision and whether people receiving the letter will understand what it means. An enthusiastic promise at a progress meeting could commit the team to releasing material it has had no opportunity to verify.

Write a short change proposal. Describe the difficulty the partner reported, the proposed addition, who would need to verify it and the effect on the planned pilot. Compare adding the information now, directing readers to a verified contact for the moment or treating the issue as separate work with its own responsible owner. Ask a colleague who knows the distinction between an appointment message and a decision notice to review the options. The project sponsor can then decide what belongs in this release and communicate how the other need will be addressed.

The One DHS area Planning and delivery includes project management and financial stewardship. Staff hours, partner review and the time needed to correct a faulty mailing all belong in the cost discussion. A decision to keep the date may be defensible if the team narrows the pilot. To release the same quantity by the same date while quietly removing an agreed access check would change the promised quality. Bring that tradeoff to the sponsor in words the people doing the checking would recognize.

teaching.title: Test the handoff from the receiving office
teaching.text:
In Make a process easier to use, start with the task a resident should be able to complete when the letter arrives. Give a colleague unfamiliar with the project the reviewed version and a realistic situation. For example, the time offered conflicts with a medical appointment. Ask the colleague to find out how to request another time and what happens if the first contact does not answer. If the letter requires a phone call, ask the receiving office what instructions it gives at that point.

Use the answers to trace a failure to the right owner. If the letter points to the wrong location, the document owner can correct it. If the instructions point to an unanswered line, a wording change alone will not resolve the difficulty. Record the remaining issue with the person authorized to handle it. Close the pilot when the receiving team can identify the approved version, the person who maintains it and the route for reporting a new problem after the project manager moves on.

scenario: Two offices are testing a revised appointment letter before a Friday handoff. A partner asks to add a second letter about rescheduling. Staff already booked the last reader-testing session and production has a narrow print window.
decision: What would you ask the sponsor to decide?

choices.label: Keep Friday's handoff for the tested letter and scope the second one with the partner for the next cycle.
choices.feedback: The tested change can reach readers on time. Ask the receiving office to confirm which version it will use and what it will tell people about rescheduling meanwhile.

choices.label: Move the handoff and test both letters together after the next print window.
choices.feedback: Testing the two letters together may catch contradictions that separate tests miss. The sponsor needs the cost of delay and an interim way for people to reschedule.

perspective: A reader brings both current letters to the test. Their phone numbers conflict. Fixing only the first could send people to the wrong team.
reconsider: What narrow change could reduce the immediate risk, who can authorize it, and what needs a later reader test?
reflection: Which part of a handoff can look finished to the project team and still be unclear at the service desk?
transfer: Write three lines for a handoff naming the approved version, unresolved question and person who can change it.
followup: Protect reader testing, name the approver and make sure the receiving office knows which version to send.

title: Evaluating a program while there is still time to change it
objective: Judge whether a pilot really worked before expanding it
learn: How to compare requests with completed work, ask whether people got useful answers, and count what the pilot cost others

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A pilot offers evening callbacks to people who cannot speak with program staff during the day. After the first month, the team reports that it completed 60 calls. A leader considering a second shift needs to know more. How many people wanted an evening call? Could they actually reach someone who could help? Did evening coverage reduce the time others could reach staff during the day? Each question points to a different piece of evidence and a different decision.

teaching.title: Start with the decision the evidence will support
teaching.text:
Before the pilot, write down the change people should experience. In this example, a useful outcome is that people who request an evening conversation can complete their next step. The number of calls placed describes staff activity. The share of people reached among those requesting a call describes access to the conversation. The share who could act afterward tells the team something about its usefulness. Decide who can collect each measure, when to collect it, and how to protect the people behind the numbers.

Capture a starting point where one exists, such as the typical time from a request to a successful contact under the earlier schedule. Agree on how to handle repeated attempts so that one person called four times does not count as four people served. If the pilot is already running, use available records and identify the gaps. Interviews and a small review of participants’ experiences can reveal where a process succeeds or breaks down, even when earlier figures are incomplete.

teaching.title: Let people help interpret the finding
teaching.text:
Suppose many evening callers are reached but few complete the next step. Ask participants and staff to describe what happened after the call. A required handoff might be available only during business hours. Invite people to discuss unexpected effects as well. A conversation at an existing community gathering or a map of effects drawn by participants can reveal consequences a fixed survey missed. People who never reached the program may need a different way to contribute.

Use what you learn during the pilot. Try an agreed handoff on one evening shift, track what happens, and report whose experience is still missing. A change over time may have several explanations. Tell the decision maker what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and what would justify expanding, revising, or ending the pilot.

teaching.title: Give the count a denominator and an honest interpretation
teaching.text:
Sixty completed calls could mean sixty residents reached once, thirty reached twice, or a mix of completed conversations and voicemails. Define a successful contact and the unit being counted before comparing shifts. Suppose 80 distinct people requested an evening callback during a pilot week. Staff reached 48 of them within the agreed window. The reach rate among people requesting that option is 60 percent. It says nothing by itself about people who needed the option and never learned it existed. A different question needs a different population.

Use Plan how to learn from results to specify the population, calculation, baseline, source of evidence and who can authorize its use. Decide what the team will do if a signal changes. If fewer people can get through during the day, the staffing pattern may need to change even if evening contacts rise. If people can answer evening calls but still have to start over the next morning, ask whether evening staff have access to the help callers actually need. Avoid collecting names in an evaluation worksheet. Where subgroup comparisons are appropriate, work with the data owner on reporting safeguards.

Build the baseline prospectively if you can. If the pilot already began, examine which comparable records exist and document any changes in definitions. An unusually busy week, a new notice or staff vacancies could account for part of a difference. Showing what happened and deciding what to try next can be worthwhile even when a causal conclusion would outrun the evidence.

teaching.title: Invite people to make sense of an unexpected result
teaching.text:
Numbers rarely explain why an option was usable. A program evaluator might join an existing partner meeting, conduct interviews or invite participants to map effects that appeared after the pilot. In a ripple effects exercise, a participant could describe being able to handle a call outside work. Another may describe a later disruption because the promised time was too vague. Trace those experiences back to a feature the team could change. Seek differing experiences, including from people whose calls were missed.

Bring a preliminary interpretation back to the people who helped produce it. Ask what the team has overlooked and who is absent from the account. Working this way while a service is still changing is a form of developmental evaluation. Record a decision such as narrowing the callback window for one week, the workload consequence to monitor and the evidence that would justify extending the change. The leader who authorized the pilot should be able to explain why the decision serves the public and what uncertainty remains.

scenario: An evening callback pilot reports 60 completed calls. A director asks to expand it across all teams. One team counted callers more than once, and the morning line lost coverage when workers moved to evenings.
decision: What evidence would justify the next decision?

choices.label: Extend the test with a consistent count of people offered a callback, reached and able to complete their next step.
choices.feedback: This gives the completion count a denominator and a service outcome. Set a limit on the test and also track what happens on the morning line.

choices.label: Ask callers who were reached whether evening calls worked better and review morning waits before deciding.
choices.feedback: People can explain why timing mattered. People who could not be reached are absent, so provide a separate route for their experience and avoid treating replies as representative.

perspective: A parent was reached twice but could not complete the next step because document review was available only during business hours.
reconsider: What did the pilot deliver for this parent? Which measure would reveal others in the same situation?
reflection: Which number in your own program can rise while the intended result stands still?
transfer: Specify the population, denominator, intended result and one possible cost elsewhere before the next pilot decision.
followup: Compare requests with completed calls, ask whether people got useful answers, and check what evening coverage cost daytime callers.

title: Making better use of workplace technology
objective: Set up a shared way to find and hand off the approved version of a document
learn: How to test a process by having a colleague retrieve, change and hand off work using the proposed steps

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: Two people can spend an afternoon correcting the same guidance and end up with two incompatible files. A faster application will do little for them until the team agrees where the working copy lives and how a colleague can recognize the approved version. Technology is most useful when staff can name a task it should make easier and check whether the person doing the task experienced an improvement.

teaching.title: Follow one piece of work
teaching.text:
Trace a common activity from request through completion. Suppose county partners submit questions ahead of an office hour. Staff copy questions out of email, group similar ones, assign speakers, and circulate revised agendas. Ask the coordinator to show where information gets retyped, where an edit gets lost, and which decisions still need a person who understands the issue. Look at features in tools already available to the team. A shared list with a topic, owner, status, and due date might resolve more of the problem than buying a new system.

Try the smallest change with a few colleagues. Give them the link from the invitation and ask them to find their assignments and update them. Include someone joining remotely and someone who navigates by keyboard. Check which information belongs in the shared space, who can view it, and who can change it. Keep identifying service details out of a general agenda. Pair a calendar reminder with a named reviewer so an automated notice does not become a substitute for a decision.

teaching.title: Teach the task and examine the result
teaching.text:
Have a colleague demonstrate how to enter a new question and find its answer. Then let another employee do it with realistic sample information. Offer short written instructions and a contact for help. Someone who uses the software daily may still need support when an update moves a familiar control. Give that colleague a useful problem to solve while practicing.

After two meetings, compare the effort to prepare the agenda and the number of questions left without an owner. Ask partners whether they can still submit a question through an accessible channel, including when their organization cannot open the shared workspace. If work merely moved from the coordinator to dozens of partners, revise the process. The measure of success is how well the whole exchange works.

teaching.title: Design a workflow that survives a lost connection
teaching.text:
To evaluate a technology choice, carry one task across offices with different working conditions. Suppose a county partner is revising a public information sheet with a DHS colleague. The partner has intermittent access to the shared workspace. The DHS editor needs the latest approved guidance and the communications reviewer needs a clean copy for publication. Agree on what the reviewers will treat as the active draft, who may change it and how someone can contribute when the shared session is unavailable.

Walk through an outage. The partner submits a correction by an approved alternative route while another editor revises the same paragraph. Who resolves the conflict? Where will the decision be recorded? Is there a way for the partner to see whether the correction survived? An agreed file name is helpful. An identified owner with enough time to review the change is more important. Automating distribution before the team has settled those questions can spread an outdated version more quickly to everyone using it.

Connect this exercise to Digital access in the One DHS competency collection and to the Plain language and accessible documents checklist. Have an employee unfamiliar with the draft try to locate the current heading, the link destination and the next action using the method they ordinarily use. Observe what happens when a digital copy becomes a printout or a downloaded PDF. If a change is visible only through colored markup, publishing the file in another format may remove its meaning.

teaching.title: Teach one feature well enough for someone else to take over
teaching.text:
Select a feature that addresses a documented difficulty. It might be version history for two people editing at different times, or a reminder for the person responsible for checking an expiring contact. An experienced user can demonstrate the feature on a practice document and then hand control to a colleague. Ask the colleague to restore a prior wording, identify the person responsible for approval and prepare the clean version. The colleague's ability to carry out the task is more informative than a demonstration led entirely by an expert.

Compare the revised workflow with the earlier one over a small number of routine changes. Count interruptions, duplicate requests and corrections made after release. Ask whether anyone now spends extra time converting a file or transcribing comments. If the burden has moved to a partner with less technical support, revisit the tool or permission settings with the appropriate owner. Retain the technique when the work is easier to complete across the whole route and the team can sustain it after the person who introduced it is away.

scenario: Staff in two offices keep different copies of referral guidance. When the shared drive is unavailable, one office uses an old attachment. Someone discovers the conflicting versions only after a resident is sent to the wrong desk.
decision: What would you change before the next revision?

choices.label: Agree on an owner, publish one dated current copy and test whether receiving staff can locate it from a normal workstation.
choices.feedback: A known location and a tested path reduce guesswork. Decide how staff should confirm current instructions when the shared location is unavailable.

choices.label: Send both offices a fresh attachment and request confirmation that everyone received it.
choices.feedback: This can resolve the current discrepancy quickly. A forwarded attachment can outlast its approval, so set an expiry or retrieval instruction and a named contact.

perspective: An evening worker has permission to read the guidance but cannot reach the owner after hours. Their backup binder holds last quarter's copy.
reconsider: What will happen on the next evening outage, and how will the owner know an obsolete copy was used?
reflection: Where could someone reliably find the current version without relying on your memory?
transfer: Ask a colleague on another shift to retrieve one approved item using only the documented route. Record any failed step and its owner.
followup: Have a colleague retrieve the current guidance, make a permitted change and hand it off using the proposed steps.
