title: Writing a grant proposal a reviewer can use
objective: Align a proposal's promises with its budget
learn: How to trace one resident need through the work plan, the partner's role, the budget and a result residents can recognize

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A convincing proposal lets a reviewer trace a line from a documented need to an activity, a budget, and a result that people can recognize. Clarity about that line also protects the people who might have to deliver the work. A promise that reads well in an application can become a difficult commitment when a partner has neither agreed to it nor been budgeted to carry it out.

teaching.title: Decide whether the opportunity fits
teaching.text:
Read the funding notice before drafting the story. Identify who may apply, what costs and activities are eligible, the period of work, required attachments, any match, submission instructions, and the selection criteria. Assign someone to resolve uncertainties early. If the funder limits eligibility to community organizations, a state team cannot assume it can lead an application. Ask the potential partner what role, if any, it wants and check what the notice permits.

Imagine an opportunity to improve residents’ access to service information. A community partner proposes evening sessions where people can try finding an answer and ask questions as they go. Learn what the funder means by improved access and what the partner has already heard from residents. Verify that the proposed session time, language support, and follow-up make sense to the intended participants. A funder’s interest and an agency’s favorite project may overlap only partly.

teaching.title: Build one account of the work
teaching.text:
Describe the barrier precisely. Explain who will prepare materials, host sessions, respond to questions, and determine whether people found what they needed. Connect each activity to a supportable cost. If the narrative promises interpretation at four events but the budget pays for two, the reader has uncovered a service decision the partners still need to make. Agree on the scope and reflect it consistently in the work plan, budget, and narrative.

Keep one file set with named owners and due dates for approvals and partner contributions. Before submitting, ask someone outside the drafting team to score the application against the notice. Have them point to the evidence for each criterion and explain, in their own words, what would change for a resident. A gap in that explanation tells you which part of the proposal still needs work while there is time to fix it.

teaching.title: Read the proposal once as the funder and once as the partner
teaching.text:
A proposal for community navigation can be convincing on its first reading and unworkable on its second. From the funder's perspective, the narrative connects residents to services and the budget pays for a navigator. From a partner's perspective, a navigator is also expected to organize meetings, arrange interpretation, make referrals, answer after-hours calls and document what happened. Determine whether those responsibilities can be delivered by the position and hours the budget describes. Ask the partner privately which promises it has the people and resources to make.

Give each requirement a place in the application. For a requirement to demonstrate community involvement, identify the work done with people affected and the choices their input actually influenced. A supportive remark at an event does not establish that an organization has agreed to recruit participants or share information. Obtain a partner's agreement to the specific role and wording before counting that contribution. If the funder's priorities and the proposed service diverge, discuss whether a different opportunity would fit better before rewriting the project to appeal to a reviewer.

In the One DHS curriculum, the finance and contracts cultural humility simulation examines applicant questions, review against published criteria and concerns after an award. Work through the applicant question from the other side of the desk. Which application requirement would a small community organization need the most time to understand? Where could an official clarification help every applicant? Bring a question through the funder's stated process. Preserve any official answer and review the draft against it.

teaching.title: Give the reviewer a traceable claim
teaching.text:
Take one sentence, such as a promise to help residents complete a referral. Name the obstacle the team has observed and how it learned about it. Describe which activity the funds would support, which role would perform it and what evidence could show whether residents completed the next step. Separate the output the applicant controls, such as offering navigation appointments, from the benefit it hopes will follow. A partner's waitlist can affect whether someone receives a service even after a successful referral.

Ask a fresh reader to trace that sentence to the budget and timetable. A translation commitment should have time for review and a realistic cost. A quarterly report should have an owner and an agreed source for its figures. If any link fails, repair the work plan as well as the prose. Before submission, use a single filed version and a record of approvals, so the people preparing to deliver a successful award can see precisely what was promised.

interaction: Audit a promise against its budget
scenario: A grant draft promises interpretation at four community sessions. The budget covers two, and the partner listed as the interpreter coordinator has only agreed to recruit participants. The writer is one day from submission.
decision: Which promise can the team responsibly make?

choices.label: Reopen the scope with the partner, price the full access plan, and ask the sponsor which funded delivery pattern can meet the outcome.
choices.feedback: Readers can trace the need to an activity, a responsible partner and a cost. Check that reducing the number of sessions preserves people's opportunity to take part.

choices.label: Keep four sessions and explore whether another cost can be shifted to interpretation before submission.
choices.feedback: This may retain the planned reach. Document what the change would displace, obtain the partner's agreement and revise the proposal if the shift cannot be confirmed.

perspective: The partner explains that two longer sessions would exclude people who can attend only briefly. A shorter repeated format might reach them within the same staff hours.
reconsider: How would you compare reach, access and cost before writing the final promise?
reflection: Which part of your proposal depends on work someone else has yet to accept?
transfer: Trace one participant need through an activity, cost, partner commitment and outcome. Flag any link without evidence.
followup: Trace one resident need through the work plan, the partner’s agreed role, the budget and a result residents can recognize.

title: Communicating clearly when you delegate
theme: Teams and the work they carry
objective: Hand off work with clear limits on what the other person can decide
learn: How to separate what someone can settle alone, what needs consultation and which promises only the sponsor can make

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: “Please coordinate the listening session” can mean booking a room to one person and designing the entire engagement to another. A supervisor who discovers the difference on the morning of the session has left an important decision unmade. Good delegation gives a colleague a result to own, the authority and resources to reach it, and a clear way to surface a problem before it lands on participants.

teaching.title: Agree on the result and the decisions
teaching.text:
Start with the purpose. Suppose a team wants people receiving services to help it choose which parts of an orientation need revision. Ask the colleague leading the session how they would gather views, whose perspective the plan might miss, and what support they need. Agree on the date, what participants should be able to influence, and how their input will get back to the person deciding. Define what a usable handoff looks like. A short account of competing priorities and unanswered questions may serve the team better than a page of attendance figures.

Match the assignment to the person’s experience and authority. A first-time facilitator might design the questions and lead a small discussion with an experienced colleague available. The supervisor may need to approve spending or make introductions to partners. Let the facilitator choose a workable method within those boundaries. If the supervisor prescribes every question and rejects every change, accountability for the session design still rests with the supervisor.

teaching.title: Stay available at the moments that matter
teaching.text:
Set a checkpoint when the colleague has a draft invitation and there is still time to change the plan. A shared document, an agreed response time, and an accessible meeting option help people working from different locations contribute. Invite written suggestions before the checkpoint. Name who resolves a disagreement if the group cannot. For a larger effort, record owners and dates in one place everyone involved can use.

Have the colleague explain what they will decide and what would prompt them to call you. Afterward, review an actual moment from the session together. Did participants understand the decision? What helped someone raise a different view? Recognize the colleague’s judgment, ask what responsibility they want next, and carry out the commitments only you have authority to make.

Before handing over an assignment, name any prescribed procedure, accessibility requirement or approval that limits how the employee can do it. Within those limits, give them room to choose a method and explain how the result will be judged. Holding someone responsible for the outcome while privately dictating every choice makes it difficult to tell whose judgment is being developed.

teaching.title: How much authority does the employee actually have
teaching.text:
A manager delegates a listening session to a colleague who has organized several internal meetings. The colleague can reserve a room but cannot authorize overtime, change a program deadline or promise that a public recommendation will be adopted. Participants may ask about all three. Agree beforehand on the language the facilitator can use to explain who holds each decision and when a response can be expected. Give the facilitator access to the responsible people, including a backup when the sponsor is unavailable.

Work with the Empowering or delegative leadership lesson. Pick one decision to transfer completely, one the facilitator can make after consultation and one the sponsor must retain. For example, the facilitator can choose how people offer comments, consult an access specialist about the format and refer a budget request to the sponsor. Consider what happens if a participant needs more time and the room reservation ends at four. A staff member with authority to open a written response period can act immediately. A staff member who has to seek approval needs a name and a response time.

Visibility complicates a first assignment. A person can learn a public-facing task without having to manage every difficult exchange alone. Offer a rehearsal with a colleague playing an impatient partner. Let the employee answer, then ask what information or authority would have helped them answer more accurately. Decide in advance when the sponsor will step in and how they will return the floor. An intervention that rescues a capable employee at every hesitation can deprive the person of the very opportunity the assignment was meant to provide.

teaching.title: Set up a record people in different places can use
teaching.text:
When a distributed team is preparing the session, a meeting, a chat and a shared document may each hold a different answer. Agree on one current record of the objective, authorized decisions, due dates and unresolved questions. Give staff a way to flag a question between meetings. Use check-ins for decisions that benefit from discussion and return the decision to the shared record so it reaches people who were away.

After the session, compare the delegated objective with what participants experienced. Did people know which decisions they could affect? Did the facilitator receive useful feedback and get credit for their work? Did the sponsor follow up on questions the facilitator was asked to refer? Use the answers to decide which responsibility the employee is prepared to take on next. Assigning someone a visible task builds capability when the experience includes authority, preparation and a fair account of the result.

scenario: A supervisor asks a colleague to lead a public listening session. The colleague can change the speaking order and invite follow-up, but a sponsor controls changes to the service process. Participants will expect an answer about evening appointments.
decision: What should the colleague be ready to decide and say during the session?

choices.label: Rehearse what they can change in the room, how to record a request and who will answer the unresolved service question by a named date.
choices.feedback: The colleague can act without waiting on every detail. Ask them to replay a difficult request so both of you hear the same boundary.

choices.label: Offer to attend and answer every difficult question while the colleague facilitates.
choices.feedback: This gives participants a ready escalation route. It can also leave the delegated lead uncertain about ordinary decisions once you step out. Agree which questions actually need you.

perspective: A participant asks for a change in next week's session time, then asks for evening appointments every week. The requests sound similar but sit with different decision owners.
reconsider: Which request can the colleague settle now? How will the participant learn what happens to the other?
reflection: What authority might a colleague reasonably infer from the words “you're in charge”?
transfer: Before the next handoff, ask the delegate to name one decision they own, one requiring consultation and a promise only the sponsor can make.
followup: Ask the colleague to explain a decision they own and a question they would bring back before the invitation goes out.

title: Cultural awareness, competence and humility
objective: Let the person define their own goals; change an assumption built into team practice
learn: How to ask about daily choices rather than assume what independence means, and how to trace a recurring assumption to the person who can change the training

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A supervisor notices that the people who stay after a meeting often shape the decision. Everyone had a chance to speak during the meeting, and the supervisor assumed that settled the question. Looking again, she realizes the team treats staying late, thinking aloud, and disagreeing on the spot as signs of engagement. People have many reasons for choosing a different way to contribute. The supervisor’s own expectations are the part she can examine first.

teaching.title: Recognize the expectation, then change a practice
teaching.text:
Cultural awareness includes recognizing the habits you bring to a situation and how much influence those habits carry in your role. Write down the observation before you interpret it. “Three people sent comments the next morning” gives you something to examine. Calling those employees indecisive tells you more about the standard you have applied. Ask how people would like to contribute and when they need to see materials to give a considered response. A cultural brief can help a leader formulate a question. The person involved can answer for their own circumstances.

Competence develops as you use what you learn. If the supervisor needs feedback on a proposal, she can distribute it in advance, invite disagreement through several channels, and name the time when the decision will close. She can use the same reasoning in a service review by asking community partners which choices are still open and which arrangements would make participation possible. Formal learning can deepen the work. A qualified administrator can help a leader use the Intercultural Development Inventory to choose a development goal. Tribal-state relations learning can prepare staff to recognize a distinct government-to-government relationship in work involving Tribal Nations.

teaching.title: Remain answerable to the people affected
teaching.text: Humility matters when someone tells you the change missed the point. Perhaps staff could send a note but decisions still followed the private conversation afterward. The supervisor can acknowledge what she allowed to happen, reopen a decision where feasible, and put the actual reasons for the next decision where the team can examine them. Ask the employees who raised the concern how the new arrangement worked, without asking any one person to speak for a whole community. Over time, their ability to influence the work is a better guide to progress than the supervisor’s confidence in her own cultural knowledge.

teaching.title: Examine the demand the institution places on a person
teaching.text:
It helps to examine whose account becomes part of a public decision. Consider a person who wants help staying near family. A staff member asks about independent living goals and records that the person has no interest in becoming more independent. The wording has shifted the meaning. The person described a relationship they want to maintain. The record interprets their preference through the staff member's idea of growth.

Several explanations remain open. The person may want more control over daily decisions while sharing a home. They may want a different arrangement and fear losing support. They may be satisfied with the current arrangement. A question that opens those possibilities is, “Which decisions about home do you want to make yourself, and whom do you want involved?” Give time for a response using the person's chosen way to communicate. With permission, include the people they identify. Keep their choices distinguishable from the worker's interpretation and from relatives' preferences.

Read the chapter Learning about communities without predicting people alongside a community brief that relates to a specific service question. Identify an assumption the reading helps you recognize in your own practice. Use it to prepare a better question for the next interaction. Because a community account can describe a historical relationship with public institutions, it may help explain why a staff practice deserves scrutiny. It cannot establish what a particular individual has experienced or what they want.

teaching.title: Move from personal learning to an organizational response
teaching.text:
Suppose a supervisor finds that several workers use the same independence question because it is the only example used in orientation. Coaching one employee can repair one encounter. The wider issue belongs to whoever maintains orientation and the planning process. Ask a small group, including people with experience of receiving support, to draft other ways to invite discussion of control, support and belonging. Show how a worker could document each preference faithfully within the current process and who can consider a change to the materials.

Cultural humility is visible in what happens after someone challenges the revised examples. A suggestion may still assume that everyone wants relatives involved. Rework it so the person can choose privacy as readily as support. Ask participants to review the wording and say what a worker would actually do differently. Revisit a small sample of practice situations after the change. Look for faithful accounts of varied choices and a clear next action the person could recognize as their own.

scenario: At a disability-services planning discussion, the team describes moving into an apartment alone as progress. Sam says they want to share a home with their sister and have her help interpret the options. Staff have yet to ask what independence means to Sam.
decision: How would you reopen the decision while protecting Sam's control?

choices.label: Ask Sam how they want their sister involved, then invite Sam to describe what a good living arrangement would make possible.
choices.feedback: Sam can define both the goal and the support. Agree on a way for Sam to correct the account, including an opportunity to speak privately if they want one.

choices.label: Ask the sister how decisions are usually made at home and then ask Sam whether that matches their preference.
choices.feedback: The sister may know practical details. Starting with her account can anchor the conversation before Sam has chosen her role. Give Sam the first opportunity to set the terms.

perspective: Sam says, “I want help weighing the costs. I want to decide who I live with.” The team's standard opening question had treated living alone as the goal before anyone spoke.
reconsider: What would you change about this meeting and the next team's opening question? How could Sam tell whether their words changed the plan?
reflection: What ordinary signal of progress in your work might carry an unexamined cultural assumption?
transfer: Try an open question about the person's goal and chosen support in a suitable conversation. Check the written account with the person through their preferred route.
followup: The person defines what support and privacy they want. Trace a recurring assumption to the person who can change the training.

title: Accessibility in documents and meetings
objective: Make an invitation and a meeting usable by everyone
learn: How to keep key details out of images, test the route by keyboard, and name who can pause a meeting if captions fail

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A resident opens an invitation to a public session. The address appears in a picture of a flyer. The registration link says “here,” and the sentence about accommodations is also part of the picture. A colleague can read everything on the screen and still miss the problem. Someone using a screen reader may have no practical way to find the address, distinguish the link, or learn whom to contact. The author can fix those barriers before the invitation goes out.

teaching.title: Publish information people can act on
teaching.text:
Begin with an accessible document template. Give the meeting a descriptive title, use built-in heading styles for sections, and put the date, time, location, and contact in ordinary text. Give a link a name that describes the action it opens. If an image conveys information, provide a text equivalent that communicates what someone needs to know. Use sufficient contrast, and label the choices in words. A calendar marked only with red and green dots leaves the meaning uncertain even if someone can distinguish the colors.

Run the accessibility checker and examine what it flags. Then try a practical task. Starting at the top, can you navigate by keyboard to the accommodation contact? If you read only the headings and links, can you identify how to register? A tool may confirm that an image has alternative text even when its description says only “graphic.” The author still has to decide whether the information makes sense.

teaching.title: Carry access through the event
teaching.text:
Include the appropriate contact for accommodation requests and an accessible way to reach them. Choose a meeting platform that supports captions and plan for any requested communication support with the people coordinating it. Provide materials in advance where possible. During a presentation, describe the trend in a chart aloud and include the figures in accessible text. Give someone joining by phone a way to participate in an exercise that others complete in chat.

Before the session, assign someone to monitor access problems and respond privately when appropriate. If the captions fail, pause so the affected participant can help identify a workable option. Afterward, ask whether people could find the materials, contribute, and receive follow-up in a usable form. Keep improvements in the template so the next organizer starts with what the team learned.

teaching.title: Rehearse the route from invitation to participation
teaching.text:
Open Make participation more accessible and follow the experience of a resident who receives the digital invitation and calls to arrange participation. Start with the contact details. Does the invitation name the person or area responsible for requests? Can someone use more than one channel if the first is difficult? Does the person answering know who arranges the support and when to respond? A well-formatted invitation can still leave a resident unable to join a conversation when the next person in the chain has no instructions.

In a rehearsal, give different participants a task rather than asking for a general opinion. One person finds the location and asks how to contribute in writing. Another joins online and locates caption controls. A facilitator explains a chart aloud in enough detail for someone to take part in the decision about it. A note-taker records a written contribution alongside one offered verbally. If a question is put to a vote, check whether all offered participation methods allow a person to weigh in before the decision closes.

The Plain language and accessible documents checklist can guide the material review. Use native headings for structure, meaningful link text, a usable reading order and sufficient contrast. Where colors identify status or options, put the meaning in words as well. Run the built-in accessibility checker and review the flags. Then use the document to perform a real task. Software can detect certain missing elements and still be unable to tell whether an image description explains the information a reader needs.

teaching.title: Give someone the authority to repair the meeting
teaching.text:
Suppose captions fail midway through the discussion. Decide in advance who can pause the meeting, arrange another way to participate and determine whether a decision needs to wait. A directive response can be appropriate when the immediate action is clear. State what is happening, take responsibility for the adjustment and explain when business will resume. Ask the participant privately what would make participation possible. They should have a choice about what to share in front of the group.

The later review belongs to the team that organized the session. Did staff know how to reach support? Did people get a chance to revisit information they missed? Was feedback through a later channel considered before the decision? Choose a repair that addresses the gap found in the rehearsal or event. A reusable meeting template can carry the corrected contact information and decision procedure into the next session. Review it again when the technology, venue or audience changes.

scenario: A public meeting invitation contains the registration link and access contact inside an image. A colleague points this out the day before the meeting. During rehearsal the caption feed also stops unexpectedly.
decision: Where will you intervene and who can act when access breaks?

choices.label: Replace the image-only details with accessible text, contact invitees through the original channels, and agree on a stop-and-recover signal with the facilitator.
choices.feedback: This repairs the invitation and gives people a route back into the live discussion. Test registration, access questions and the meeting connection with a second person.

choices.label: Prepare an accessible recording and written response form for people who cannot participate live.
choices.feedback: A later route can be valuable. Identify which decisions participants could influence afterward and protect a live route for people who want a voice before the decision.

perspective: A participant explains they could read the meeting date but never found the registration link. Another participant needs captions during discussion to challenge a proposal before it is adopted.
reconsider: What has to happen before any decision, and how will someone who missed the invitation learn about the change?
reflection: At which step in the participant journey did your last accessibility check end?
transfer: Walk one invitation from discovery to participation and response. Record a responsible person and recovery step for the first point of failure.
followup: Rehearse the whole route from finding the contact by keyboard to contributing before the decision closes.

title: Practicing allyship where you have influence
objective: Respond when someone points out that opportunities go to a small group; change the next selection
learn: How to ask how the person wants to be involved, and how to check who got notice, preparation and time to compete

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A unit selects people for temporary project lead assignments through informal recommendations. The assignments build the experience supervisors look for in later selection decisions. An employee points out that the same small circle keeps hearing about them first. The manager who receives that concern has standing to ask how assignments are made. That standing gives her a way to act even though the existing arrangement has worked well for her personally.

teaching.title: Examine who can enter and who sets the rules
teaching.text:
Look at how someone actually becomes a candidate. Who hears about the work? Who can put a name forward? What counts as evidence that a person can lead? Which staff have previously been given a chance to produce that evidence? A criterion that sounds reasonable can keep rewarding earlier access. Ask how exceptions are granted, who can challenge a decision, and whether people face different consequences for doing so. A pattern deserves examination even when nobody has made an openly exclusionary remark.

Speak with the person who raised the concern about what support would be useful and what they want kept private. They may want to present the issue themselves, ask for an introduction, or prefer that management examine its own procedures without identifying them. Take responsibility for finding information you can obtain yourself. A colleague should be able to raise a barrier without becoming the unpaid coordinator of the entire response.

teaching.title: Use your authority and account for the result
teaching.text:
The manager could bring the assignment process to the group that controls it, propose publishing the duties and selection criteria, and arrange coverage so interested staff can take part. If a colleague has developed a workable approach and wants to present it, introduce them as its author and make room for them to answer questions. The manager can handle objections about staffing that require a management decision.

Return after the next assignment cycle. Did more people hear about the opening in time? Could an employee who was passed over find out what experience would help next time? Ask whether the change made participation easier and what barriers remain. People affected by the arrangement can judge the value of the support. Following their feedback through a second decision often demands more commitment than speaking up at the first one.

teaching.title: Distinguish a sponsorship decision from a conduct concern
teaching.text:
The common case Who gets the visible work? in the leadership styles pathway asks learners to examine both an allocation pattern and what happened when an employee challenged it. Those issues can have different owners and consequences. A person interrupted during a discussion may need immediate support. They may also want the manager to review who gets invited to represent the unit. Correcting the interruption in the next meeting leaves the opportunity structure intact. Changing an invitation list would leave a serious conduct concern unanswered.

Try writing two responses. In the first, step in during the meeting to return the floor and give the employee credit for the point they made. In the second, speak privately afterward. Ask what support the person wants, explain which decisions belong to the supervisor and clarify how any conduct issue will reach the appropriate authorized process. Avoid promises about confidentiality or the outcome that exceed your authority. A colleague acting as an ally can offer to support the employee while allowing them to speak in their own words.

Next, investigate how visible assignments move from a supervisor's desk to a person's workload. Recruitment by informal conversation can favor staff who work nearby, have time to volunteer or already know a temporary opportunity is likely. People who have covered difficult work behind the scenes may have relevant qualifications that remain unseen. Examine how eligibility was defined, who learned about the assignment, who had preparation and what decisions were documented. Respect privacy as you trace the procedure.

teaching.title: Use influence where a decision can change
teaching.text:
The Transformative or equity-centered leadership lesson invites attention to how a system distributes opportunity. In this case, a supervisor might publish selection criteria, offer practice for first-time presenters and account for coverage on staff schedules. Consider who will still be excluded. Employees working a late shift might see a notice only after a slot is full. A rotation may distribute turns but leave all the coaching with one person. Ask staff privately how they learned about the opportunity and what would have made participation feasible.

Agree on a review point after enough assignments have been made to examine a pattern. Record which parts the supervisor can change now and which decisions require another authority. Share the changes and the reason for them in a way that avoids identifying whoever first raised the concern. Ask the people the change was meant to support whether it gave them a choice they could use. Acting as an ally involves accepting that their answer may differ from the leader's assessment of the effort.

interaction: Act on a pattern without exposing a colleague
scenario: A coworker privately says acting assignments keep going to the same small group on day shift. They want access to development but do not want to be identified. You can influence the process for the next opportunity.
decision: How can you use your influence before the next name is chosen?

choices.label: With the coworker's permission, raise the selection process without identifying them. Propose published criteria, notice across shifts, and a way to offer evidence from less visible work.
choices.feedback: The proposal can change access beyond one appointment. Check timing, coverage and who can actually approve changes. Report the response through the coworker's preferred route.

choices.label: Offer to nominate the coworker at the next selection meeting after asking whether they want the nomination.
choices.feedback: Personal sponsorship may help if they want it. Telling their story or nominating them without permission risks exposing their concern and leaves the access pattern intact.

perspective: The coworker says a nomination is welcome later. This month their shift cannot attend the preparation session, and other workers have the same conflict.
reconsider: Which feature of the next assignment could you change without using anyone's personal account?
reflection: When has access depended on having someone willing to speak for you?
transfer: Before the next opportunity, check who can receive notice, prepare and provide evidence. Take one concrete change to the person who controls it.
followup: Ask how the worker wants to be involved. Check who actually got notice, preparation and time to compete.

title: Creating a culture of inclusion
objective: Correct an account of support so it reflects what staff actually said
learn: How to let contributors check how their input was reported and tell them who will answer the open question

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: A team invites employees to comment on a proposed service change. During the meeting, staff who answer public calls describe a problem with the revised instructions. Later, the decision memo credits the design group and says employees broadly supported the plan. The invitation was open. The record still erased both the concern and the people who raised it. Inclusion becomes visible in what happens to a contribution after someone makes it.

teaching.title: Widen the ways people can contribute
teaching.text:
Explain what people can influence, circulate enough information to think about the question, and use language that gives everyone a way in. Address a group as colleagues or participants. Use the names and pronouns people share. Give directions people can follow whether they use speech, chat, a keyboard, or a mobility aid. A team might say, “The service desk is on the first floor beside the elevators,” so someone can choose a route that works for them. Invite comments privately or in writing as well as during the meeting.

Ask whose knowledge the decision requires. Bring the people doing the work into the discussion at a stage when their experience can change its direction. A senior participant can help by crediting a colleague’s observation by name when appropriate and giving the colleague room to explain it. If someone mocks a question or dismisses an accent, the meeting leader can interrupt, identify the disrespectful behavior, and return the discussion to the person’s point. Follow up through the appropriate workplace process when further action is needed.

teaching.title: Show people what became of their contribution
teaching.text:
In the service-change example, the meeting leader can ask the employees to check the account of the problem and invite a different view from staff who read the memo later. The decision owner can explain which instruction will change, who will test the revision, and why another suggestion cannot be adopted now. If the memo misattributed the work, correct the record and share the corrected version with its recipients.

Over several decisions, look for a pattern. Do the same voices carry formal credit while other staff supply evidence in private? Do people learn what happened only if they attend an optional event? Adjust how decisions are recorded and communicated. Trust has a concrete basis when employees can raise a hard point, recognize it in the record, and see who took responsibility for acting on it.

teaching.title: Give disagreements a place in the decision record
teaching.text:
An invitation to contribute has little value if a staff member's concern disappears between the conversation and the final recommendation. A leader can interrupt that pattern while a decision is being made. Put the question in plain language, explain what is still open, and invite different accounts of what might happen after release. Give contributors a chance to check the account of what they said. If people disagree, record the specific point of disagreement and what would help resolve it.

Try this with a public message about a change in service hours. A communications specialist wants a short announcement. A front-desk worker knows callers will ask how to reach someone outside the new hours. A community partner points out that people may depend on a contact who is no longer available. These three people have identified different tasks the message needs to support. Combine an accessible announcement with clear details about what happens when the office is closed, then ask each contributor to try it on the situation they described.

Use Inclusive leadership alongside Democratic or participative leadership in the leadership styles collection. Rehearse two versions of the decision meeting. In the first, everyone has equal speaking time but only the manager decides what is recorded. In the second, participants can offer written comments, review the options and correct the record before the manager makes the choice. Ask who could influence the outcome in each version and which conditions made their expertise visible. A vote can be useful for some choices. It is a poor way to decide whether an individual experienced exclusion.

teaching.title: Make trust visible after the decision
teaching.text:
Language matters throughout this work. An invitation that addresses “everyone,” names the task and explains ways to participate gives people less to infer about whether they belong. Credit the person or group responsible for an improvement, checking their preferences when a public acknowledgment would identify someone who raised a sensitive concern. If a supervisor uses inaccurate wording or overlooks a contribution, correct the record while the people affected can still use the correction.

Use Find out what changed in practice after the revised message goes out. Ask whether staff could give a usable answer to the after-hours question and whether the partner agrees that the revised directions reflect the concern. Share what the team learned and what it will revisit. Over several decisions, look for who is consistently consulted early enough to influence the options. If one unit only gets invited to comment after decisions appear settled, change when it enters the process as well as how its staff are invited.

scenario: A memo ahead of a decision on service hours says staff broadly support the change. Front-desk workers actually said the later hours could help callers and raised an unresolved concern about coverage. The announcement is due tomorrow.
decision: How would you correct the account while there is time to change the decision?

choices.label: Ask the memo owner to distinguish support for the aim from the coverage concern and confirm that wording with the staff who raised it.
choices.feedback: The decision-maker sees both pieces of evidence. Name who will resolve coverage and when staff will hear the answer.

choices.label: Ask the decision-maker for a short meeting with front-desk staff before approving the announcement.
choices.feedback: Direct contact may surface details the memo missed. Offer another route for staff on duty and correct the written account so later readers see the same evidence.

perspective: One worker says, “I want people to reach us later. I also want someone at the desk when the late shift takes a break.” They had never been asked to vote on the proposal.
reconsider: How should the decision record preserve that distinction? What commitment can the decision owner make before the announcement?
reflection: When could a reader mistake a group's participation for its endorsement?
transfer: Review a recent decision summary for one unresolved concern, its owner and the date people affected can expect an answer.
followup: Let the contributors check the account. Explain who will address the after-hours question and how staff will hear back.

title: Using pronouns respectfully
objective: Introduce a colleague respectfully when the right wording is unclear
learn: How to use a person's name when unsure, and how to ask privately how they wish to be introduced in a setting

teaching.title: The decision in practice
teaching.text: You are about to introduce a colleague who will lead a discussion with community partners. You know the person’s name and role. You have heard colleagues use different pronouns for them. The introduction needs a few ordinary, accurate words. “Jordan Lee will lead today’s discussion. Jordan coordinates the partner meetings” works while you find a suitable opportunity to check how the person would like to be introduced.

teaching.title: Ask in a way that leaves room to choose
teaching.text:
Pronouns such as she, he, and they let us refer to a person without repeating a name. Someone’s name, voice, or appearance cannot reliably tell you which pronouns they use. If it is relevant, ask the person privately, or offer your own pronouns when making an introduction. A simple question is enough. “How would you like me to introduce you to this group?” gives Jordan room to mention pronunciation, pronouns, title, or simply the name that should appear on the agenda.

People may choose different ways of introducing themselves in different settings. If someone has told you their pronouns in a private conversation, check how they want you to refer to them with the public or in written materials when the setting is uncertain. Give participants the option of sharing pronouns during introductions. Include anyone who chooses to pass and keep the meeting moving. A colleague should be able to participate fully without explaining a personal decision.

teaching.title: Use what the person shares and repair a mistake
teaching.text:
Once Jordan shares that they use they and them with the group, practice with a sentence tied to the work. “Jordan reviewed the questions. They will invite partners to speak first.” If you use the wrong pronoun, offer a brief apology, correct the phrase, and continue. An extended explanation can leave your colleague trying to reassure you in front of an audience. If an incorrect introduction was sent in writing, ask how best to correct it and reach the people who received it.

Supervisors shape what happens after the correction. Use the right pronouns yourself, attend to repeated disrespect, and follow up with the employee about support. Staff can build fluency privately, using ordinary work sentences until the words come naturally. Everyday use spares the person the burden of correcting the same mistake at every meeting.

teaching.title: Distinguish the person's words from a workplace assumption
teaching.text:
Before a public meeting, an organizer may receive a biography, a directory entry and an introduction from another team. Each may have been written for a different audience or at a different time. Use the wording the speaker supplied for this event when it is available. When materials differ, contact the speaker privately with a practical question about the introduction. They may provide pronouns, ask to use a name throughout, or simply approve a short introduction. Organizers can prepare accurately while giving the speaker authority over how much personal information to share.

Consider a supervisor preparing to introduce Jordan to a community group. The agenda will be posted publicly, but the planning email stayed within a small team. A colleague suggests putting pronouns after every name to show that the event is welcoming. An inclusive response gives each presenter the opportunity to supply the wording used publicly. That allows presenters to share what they choose without making disclosure a condition of appearing on the agenda. It also removes the need for staff to infer anything from a person's voice, clothing or name.

Practice writing complete sentences in the context of the person's work. If someone uses they and them, rehearse both a subject and an object sentence about the work they will lead. Say the sentences aloud until they sound ordinary. Practice with invented examples or in your own notes. A colleague who has supplied their pronouns has already provided the information needed and need not coach the rest of the team.

teaching.title: Decide what an appropriate correction requires
teaching.text:
A spoken mistake in an introduction can usually be corrected at once. A mistake in an invitation that was sent to multiple organizations raises another question. Which correction will reach the people who need accurate information while respecting the speaker's wishes? Talk privately with the speaker where possible. A corrected agenda may suffice. A public explanation about a private matter could create a new problem. Ask the person who manages the event materials to check where the outdated version was also posted.

Use Ethical leadership in the leadership styles collection to examine a harder case in which someone repeatedly dismisses a colleague's correction. Describe the observable behavior and its effect on participation. A supervisor can restate the expectation for respectful conduct, offer appropriate support privately and follow the workplace process that fits the concern. Staff should not have to settle the matter in a public debate. In a rehearsal, judge the supervisor's response by whether it protects the colleague's dignity, corrects the working practice and gives the person a reliable route for follow-up. The colleague's willingness to explain their identity is unrelated to the supervisor's responsibility to act.

scenario: You will introduce a colleague to partner agencies. Their current internal email and an older public biography use different pronouns. The agenda goes out soon. You do not know which wording they want in that setting.
decision: How will you prepare the agenda and introduction?

choices.label: Use the colleague's name in the agenda. Ask privately what introduction they want for this audience and whether anything should be shared publicly.
choices.feedback: The colleague controls what is disclosed and can choose a short introduction. Leave space for a reply without making disclosure a condition of taking part.

choices.label: Send the colleague the full proposed introduction privately and invite edits before it is shared.
choices.feedback: Reviewing all the wording can feel routine. Use their name while drafting and check which details are appropriate for this audience rather than copying details into a public version.

perspective: The colleague asks you to use their name at the event and says the old biography will be updated later. A panelist inadvertently uses the earlier wording.
reconsider: How can you make a brief correction consistent with what the colleague requested and return attention to their contribution?
reflection: Where could an ordinary publishing step disclose information someone chose to share in a different setting?
transfer: Prepare one introduction using a person's preferred public wording. Identify who can update the program if a person requests a change.
followup: Use the person’s name while uncertain. If clarification matters, ask privately how they wish to be introduced in this setting.
